Te puede interesar

Reseña de “Border”: Un romance monstruoso entre lo bizarro y lo sublime

Border: La película de fantasía nórdica que tenés que ver

Te contamos porqué debes ver “Border”, la extraña y atrapante película de Ali Abassi

Border (también conocida como Gräns ) irrumpió en la pantalla en el año 2018 bajo la dirección de Ali Abbasi. Esta extraordinaria rareza sueca, inspirada en un cuento homónimo de John Ajvide Lindqvist (“Déjame entrar”), te transporta a un mundo parecido al nuestro, pero del que seguro vas a dudar. Es un territorio donde el drama, la fantasía y el suspenso se entrelazan de manera visceral, fusionando el realismo mágico y el folklore nórdico para crear una experiencia que atrae y aterra al mismo tiempo.

¿De qué va?

La historia sigue a Tina, una agente de aduanas que trabaja en un puesto fronterizo y posee un don único: puede oler las emociones de las personas. Un día, durante un control de seguridad, interroga a un hombre de traje. Revisa minuciosamente su bolso, pero no encuentra ningún objeto prohibido. Entonces le pide que saque su teléfono. Lo toma y comienza a olerlo. Algo no está bien: percibe algo oscuro. Decide seguir interrogándolo y, finalmente, descubren una tarjeta de memoria escondida en la funda. Dentro hay videos de crímenes. Una vez más, su olfato no se había equivocado. A lo largo de su vida, Tina ha sido discriminada por su apariencia y aprendió a mantenerse alejada de los demás, refugiándose en la soledad del bosque. Pero todo cambia cuando conoce a Vore, un hombre con características muy similares a las suyas.

A partir de ese encuentro, comienza a descubrir que hay mucho más detrás de su apariencia y de sus extrañas habilidades.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Three-time Oscar nominee Ralph Fiennes is reuniting with Conclave producer Tessa Ross and A Bigger Splash backer Studiocanal on Unbeaten , a biopic of legendary British horse racing trainer Henry Cecil and his most famous charge, Frankel.

Fiennes will star as Cecil and serve as executive producer on the film, which is being lined up to shoot next year.

The screenplay from Boardwalk Empire WGA nominee Bash Doran, the consulting producer on Beef , will be directed by BAFTA winner Nora Fingscheidt ( System Crasher ) with Ross producing for House Productions and Rory Aitken producing for Escapade Pictures. 42 will also produce. Pic has been developed with support from BBC Film and Conclave and The Zone of Interest backer Access Entertainment.

Related Stories

Ralph Fiennes, Colin Farrell & Wagner Moura Set For Comedy 'Art' From Director Fernando Meirelles & Screenwriter Christopher Hampton; 193 Launches For Cannes Market

Ralph Fiennes, Viggo Mortensen, Charlotte Rampling, Katherine Langford & More Set For István Szabó's 'Embers'; Filming Underway & First Looks Revealed With Embankment Aboard For Cannes Market

Studiocanal is fully financing the film and will release theatrically in its territories of the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Benelux, Australia and New Zealand. Executive producers include Anna Marsh, Ron Halpern and Joe Naftalin for Studiocanal, as well as Fiennes and Doran. Studiocanal is handling worldwide sales.

Watch on Deadline

Cecil, knighted by the Queen in 2011, was one of horse racing’s most recognizable and celebrated global figures, a 10-time champion trainer in the UK. The undefeated Frankel was his most famous horse, winning 10 Group 1 races. Many consider the horse to be the greatest European thoroughbred ever and a rival to U.S. champ Secretariat.

The film will follow the late Cecil’s bittersweet final years as he triumphantly rebuilds his career and life after suffering personal heartbreak, tabloid scandal, health crises and falling out with the industry’s most powerful owner. The relationship with Frankel and rekindling with his third wife Jane McKeown were key to his return to the top of his sport.

Tony Rushmer, author of The Triumph of Henry Cecil: The Authorized Biography , is a consultant on the film.

“I knew nothing about the legendary Henry Cecil until I read Bash Doran’s screenplay,” Fiennes said. “I was compelled and moved by it and by Henry’s story with the great horse Frankel. Henry was — and still is — a unique figure, complex and competitive in the very specific world of horse racing. I’m delighted to be reunited with Tessa Ross (producer) and to be working alongside Rory Aitken (producer) and Studiocanal. I’m particularly excited to be collaborating with Nora Fingscheidt. Her intensely immersive approach and desire for authenticity is inspiring. I was blown away by her film The Outrun .”

The project marks the second collaboration between Berlin Silver Bear winner Fingscheidt and Euro studio Studiocanal following the UK release of BAFTA-nominated The Outrun , starring Saoirse Ronan.

Fiennes is repped by 42 Management and Production, CAA and SOWDLLP. Fingscheidt is with Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, Ilene Feldman Management and Homebase. Doran is repped by UTA, Untitled and Schreck Rose.

article_text:
Films and events

Official Competition

Act 3

The latest in Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor’s series of cinematic essays is a rich and thought-provoking journey through ageing, legacy and the intersection between artistic and personal relationships.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriters Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor

Ireland-UK 2026. 83min

Courtesy of Desperate Optimists

Language English

Access information

Thursday 15 October 17:00

Audio description

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Molloy and Lawlor (Baltimore, LFF 2023) engage in a witty and moving conversation that explores family history and their latest project, a film about groundbreaking artists Claude Cahun and Marcel Moore. As they analyse this decades-long relationship, they identify parallels between these two artists and their own lives. Act 3 celebrates the power of connection, artistic exploration and the importance of memory to shape our present and future.

Grace Barber-Plentie

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The History of Concrete

Having attended a Hallmark movie workshop, John Wilson applies his learnings to a documentary about concrete, albeit with a dryly funny and deceptively understated tone.

Dependence

A filmmaker sifts through decades of home movies to understand her father, in this intimate study of what it means to love an addict.

All About the Money

The heir of one of America’s wealthiest families, who has ambitions to rebel against values he now despises, is the subject of Sinéad O’Shea’s compelling documentary portrait.

article_text:
DJs, Konzerte und Audioinstallationen spielen in der Kunstwelt eine immer größere Rolle. Versuchen die Institutionen, aus einer lukrativen Branche Kapital zu schlagen, oder verschleiert die Musik einen größeren Widerspruch?

Musik ist in der Kunstwelt gerade allgegenwärtig. Institutionen nehmen Konzerte in ihre Programme auf, und namentlich angekündigte DJs sind mittlerweile fester Bestandteil der meisten Kunstveranstaltungen und Vernissagen. Ich stelle fest, dass es immer seltener vorkommt, eine Gruppenausstellung zu sehen, bei der Künstler keine Musik in ihre Arbeiten integriert haben.

Auf der diesjährigen Biennale in Venedig, die den Titel "In Minor Keys" trug, hatten zahlreiche Länderpavillons eine musikalische Komponente. In Berlin lockten in den letzten Sommern kostenlose DJ-Nächte im Hamburger Bahnhof 200.000 Besucher an. Und die Documenta 16 , die am 12. Juni 2027 eröffnet wird, soll Gerüchten zufolge einen besonderen Schwerpunkt auf Klang legen, wie bereits auf ihrer Website angedeutet wird. Dient die plötzliche Verbreitung von Musik dazu, dem Künstlerischen etwas hinzuzufügen – oder soll sie etwas kompensieren, was die zeitgenössische Kunst nicht bieten kann?

Mir scheint es, als ob manche Künstlerinnen und Künstler Musik als atmosphärisches Mittel nutzen, um unsere schrumpfende Aufmerksamkeitsspanne aufrechtzuerhalten, wobei kaum ein theoretischer Bezug zum Werk besteht. Ich verstehe, warum: Die Kunstwelt ist übersättigt. Vernissagen, Messen und Biennalen gehen in die Hunderte, und die Werke verschwimmen schnell miteinander.

Gegenmittel für die eigene Gelassenheit

Musik kann die Müdigkeit vertreiben. Sie hilft, sich auf ein Werk zu konzentrieren, und – was noch wichtiger ist – sie erleichtert es, eine emotionale Verbindung zur Arbeit herzustellen, ganz gleich, ob man zum ersten Mal dabei oder ein abgebrühter Profi ist (beobachten Sie mal eine Gruppe von Kunstleuten beim Karaokesingen, und Sie werden sehen, wie dringend die Kunstwelt ein Gegenmittel für ihre eigene Gelassenheit braucht).

Ich glaube jedoch, dass die tiefere Ursache mit unserem heutigen Verständnis von Konzeptkunst zusammenhängt. In den späten 1960er-Jahren schufen Künstler wie Sol LeWitt und Lawrence Weiner Werke auf der Grundlage einfacher Anweisungen und einzelner Sätze. Die Idee dahinter war, dass jeder sie verstehen konnte. Ein halbes Jahrhundert später ist "konzeptuell" eher zu einem undurchsichtigen Füllwort geworden.

Die Ironie dabei ist, dass Kunst noch nie so viele Worte gebraucht hat. Präsentationen, Pressetexte und Wandtexte buhlen mit Schlagwörtern und "International Art English" um unsere Aufmerksamkeit. Irgendwann hat sich die Kunst von einem Ansatz, der darauf verzichtete, unsere Intuition allzu direkt anzusprechen, hin zu einem Ansatz entwickelt, der aktiv gegen unsere Intuition arbeitet, um als konzeptuell zu gelten.

Von Angesicht zu Angesicht

Alles wird als Referenz benutzt, doch nichts wird unmittelbar und direkt angesprochen. Eine intuitive Erklärung für jedes einzelne Kunstwerk oder jede Ausstellung existiert theoretisch, wird aber selten explizit formuliert. In diesem Sinne fand ich Führungen schon immer spannender als Ausstellungstexte. Ein Guide muss direkt sein, beschreiben, was man gerade betrachtet, und gleichzeitig den größeren Kontext mit einer gewissen Offenheit vermitteln, da er einem von Angesicht zu Angesicht gegenübersteht. Dennoch wäre es undenkbar, wenn nicht sogar peinlich, diese Führung als Wandtext zu verfassen.

Hier kommt die Musik ins Spiel. Sie kann jene Verbundenheit und Unmittelbarkeit bieten, die in der Kunstwelt heutzutage zunehmend fehlt. Musik ist oft emotional geprägt. Selbst die anspruchsvollste Komposition kann jemanden ohne musikalische Vorkenntnisse ansprechen.

Diese Anziehungskraft erklärt, warum Institutionen mittlerweile regelmäßig Musikveranstaltungen buchen – von DJs bei Eröffnungen bis hin zu eigenständigen Konzerten –, die parallel zu ihrem Kernprogramm stattfinden. Die Menschen sind bereit, Hunderte von Euro zu investieren, um eine Band live zu sehen. Für Kunstinstitutionen, die selten finanziell tragfähig sind, wäre es schwierig, von den Besuchern einen Preis für eine Ausstellung oder eine Performance zu verlangen, der auch nur annähernd dem einer Konzertkarte entspricht.

Haben Museen Angst vor ihrem eigenen Publikum?

Dennoch wollen (und sollten) Institutionen nicht zu Konzertlocations oder Clubs werden. Die jüngste Ära der Blockbuster zeigt allerdings, dass sie die Anziehungskraft großer Menschenmengen nutzen wollen, ohne sich dabei der Demütigung auszusetzen, zu reiner "Unterhaltung" zu verkommen.

Das Seltsame daran ist, dass diese Institutionen gleichzeitig zunehmend Angst vor ihrem eigenen Publikum haben. Seit Jahren ist Vorsicht in der Kunstwelt die Regel. Eine polarisierende Ausstellung oder ein ungeschickter Beitrag kann zu einem Skandal eskalieren, weshalb Programme immer wieder auf alles überprüft werden, was möglicherweise eine Gegenreaktion auslösen könnte.

Dieselben Museen, die versuchen, ein breiteres Publikum anzusprechen, wehren sich zugleich dagegen. Diese beiden Reaktionen scheinen zunächst zu unterschiedlichen Institutionen zu gehören, doch zusammen machen sie Musik zur perfekten Ergänzung für jedes öffentliche Programm. Sie zieht das Publikum an, ohne ein Risiko einzugehen. Musik kann natürlich politisch sein, doch aus institutioneller Sicht ist es weitaus unwahrscheinlicher, dass sie Anstoß erregt, falsch interpretiert oder zum Gegenstand von Protesten wird. Was auch immer Musik in Galerien bewirkt, ihr Erfolg sollte nicht mit einer Antwort auf die Widersprüche der Kunstwelt selbst verwechselt werden.

title_original: The Rouen Normandy Photography Center : An Animal History of the Children’s Photobook
editorial_title_zh: 鲁昂诺曼底摄影中心：儿童摄影书的动物史
editorial_excerpt_zh: 鲁昂诺曼底摄影中心呈现了一部儿童摄影书的动物史。本文最初发表于《摄影之眼》杂志。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "《儿童摄影书的动物史》是鲁昂诺曼底摄影中心为我们准备的展览：这是一场与多米尼克·达尔布瓦（Dominique Darbois）、罗贝尔·杜瓦诺（Robert Doisneau）、夏尔·弗雷热（Charles Fréger）、弗兰克·霍瓦特（Franck Horvat）、泽维尔·朗布尔（Xavier Lambours）、泰蕾兹·勒普拉（Thérèse Le Prat）、马克·里布（Marc Riboud）、亚历山大·罗琴科（Alexander Rodchenko）、托米·昂热雷（Tomi Ungerer）、伊拉（Ylla）以及许多其他创作者同行的旅程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“通过叙事绘本、图画书、字母书、摄影故事、纪实画册和艺术家书，两位策展人洛朗丝·勒盖恩（Laurence Le Guen）和拉法埃尔·斯托平（Raphaëlle Stopin）呈现了黑白摄影随笔、工作室定格照、摆拍摄景、拼贴画、蒙太奇以及经数字修饰或绘制的图像。这展现了儿童读物具有诗意、虚构和实验性的本质——一个通过摄影建立的真正的教育实验室。对于老少读者而言，这是一场庆祝摄影诞生两百周年的高水准盛会。”——弗朗索瓦丝·德努瓦耶（Françoise Denoyelle）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pleins les yeux ! article_text:
An Animal History of the Children’s Photobook, that’s what the Rouen Normandy Photography Center has in store for us: a journey in the company of Dominique Darbois, Robert Doisneau, Charles Fréger, Franck Horvat, Xavier Lambours, Thérèse Le Prat, Marc Riboud, Alexander Rodchenko, Tomi Ungerer, Ylla, and many others.

“Through narrative picture books, picture albums, alphabet books, photographic stories, documentary albums, and artists’ books, the two curators, Laurence Le Guen and Raphaëlle Stopin, present black-and-white photo essays, studio shots, staged scenes, collages, photomontages, and digitally retouched or painted images. A demonstration of the poetic, fictional, and experimental nature of children’s books—a true educational laboratory through photography. A high-caliber celebration of the bicentennial of photography for young and old alike.” — Françoise Denoyelle

Pleins les yeux ! Une histoire animale du livre photographique pour enfants , Centre Photographique Rouen Normandie 15 rue de la Chaîne, Rouen From October 10 to January 30, 2027 centrephotographique.com

article_text:
Il 23 maggio 2026 Marisa Merz avrebbe compiuto cento anni. Nata a Torino nel 1926 e scomparsa nella stessa città nel 2019, Maria Luisa Truccato è stata una figura centrale dell’ Arte Povera , pur mantenendo una posizione difficilmente assimilabile a quella degli altri protagonisti del movimento. La sua ricerca ha attraversato scultura, installazione, disegno e pittura, facendo ricorso a materiali e procedimenti diversi e senza stabilizzarsi in un linguaggio definitivo. In occasione del centenario, Torino le dedica Marisa Merz – La danza delle ore , una retrospettiva articolata in tre sedi, il Castello di Rivoli , la Fondazione Merz e la GAM – Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea , in programma dal 29 ottobre 2026 al 4 aprile 2027. I tre percorsi affrontano aspetti differenti del suo lavoro, dal processo creativo alla dimensione domestica, fino al rapporto tra spazio fisico e dimensione metafisica.

Celebrata in una grande esposizione alla Serpentine Gallery di Londra nel 2013, nello stesso anno è stata insignita del Leone d’Oro alla carriera, in occasione della 55ª Biennale di Venezia. È scomparsa all’età di 93 anni, con una carriera lunghissima alle spalle e una firma profondamente poetica e artigiana: biennali, quadriennali, documenta nell’82, Identité italienne al Pompidou, personali al Madre di Napoli, allo Stedelijk di Amsterdam, a Winterthur in Svizzera. Aspettando questa grande retrospettiva nella città che le ha dato i natali e che l’ha lanciata a livello internazionale, ecco cinque curiosità sulla sua vita e sulla sua opera.

È stata l’unica protagonista femminile dell’Arte Povera

Quando si parla di Arte Povera, il riferimento va generalmente a una costellazione di artisti che, a partire dalla seconda metà degli anni Sessanta, hanno messo in discussione i linguaggi e i materiali tradizionali dell’arte. La definizione, coniata da Germano Celant nel 1967, riuniva esperienze diverse, accomunate dall’interesse per la materia, i processi naturali e gli oggetti quotidiani. Tra i nomi più noti figurano Michelangelo Pistoletto , Jannis Kounellis , Giovanni Anselmo , Alighiero Boetti e Luciano Fabro .

Marisa Merz è stata l’unica protagonista femminile riconosciuta all’interno del gruppo. Presenza che in ogni caso non può essere ridotta a una questione di rappresentanza, ma che si è sempre distinta per un percorso autonomo, guidato dalla sperimentazione materiale e da una dimensione fortemente privata e restituita con un tono universale. Mentre il dibattito sull’Arte Povera si concentrava anche sulla ridefinizione dell’opera e del suo rapporto con lo spazio, Merz sviluppava quindi una ricerca in cui il fare artistico poteva partire da un’attività apparentemente ordinaria, che non si separava nettamente dall’esperienza quotidiana. Il suo lavoro si colloca così all’interno del movimento, ma ne mette in evidenza anche alcune zone meno esplorate.

L’alluminio è stato uno dei materiali centrali e più iconici della sua ricerca

Nel 1966, Marisa Merz realizza opere in sottili lamine di alluminio, un materiale leggero e duttile che permette di costruire forme instabili, capaci di modificare la percezione dello spazio: è l’inizio di una ricerca che considera la scultura come un organismo aperto alle trasformazioni, che mette in discussione l’idea della scultura come struttura compatta e definitiva.

A questo primo nucleo appartiene Living Sculpture , del 1966, opera conservata nelle collezioni della GAM di Torino che sarà presentata al pubblico dopo un intervento di restauro in occasione della retrospettiva. Il titolo stesso suggerisce una concezione della scultura ben lontana dall’idea di oggetto immobile; la materia sembra acquistare una propria vitalità, mentre la forma dipende dalle relazioni che si instaurano con lo spazio circostante.

Negli anni successivi, l’artista lavora anche con fili di rame, lana, nylon, cera e altri materiali malleabili, lavorando sulle possibilità di questi materiali di costruire trame e intrecci, mettendo al centro gesto manuale e la ripetizione.

La casa e la vita quotidiana sono parte integrante del suo lavoro

Come brevemente accennato sopra, nella ricerca di Merz il confine tra spazio domestico e spazio dell’arte rimane mobile e totalmente malleabile di volta in volta. Attività legate alla vita quotidiana e oggetti personali entrano nelle opere senza essere trasformati in forme monumentali o ricondotti a una composizione chiusa. Un passaggio significativo si verifica in questo senso nel 1968, quando l’artista partecipa ad Arte povera + Azioni povere , manifestazione organizzata ad Amalfi durante la quale Merz ha presentato sulla spiaggia coperte arrotolate e imballate con filo di rame o scotch ( Senza Titolo ) e opere legate all’infanzia della figlia Beatrice realizzate con filo di nylon, rame o lana, tra cui Scarpette e Bea.

Negli anni Settanta questa dimensione si sviluppa anche attraverso installazioni che riuniscono opere precedenti e nuovi elementi, distribuendoli nello spazio. In lavori come Ad occhi chiusi gli occhi sono straordinariamente aperti del 1975, l’assemblaggio contribuisce a costruire un ambiente in cui il rapporto tra pubblico e privato non è più definito da una separazione netta. La casa, in questa prospettiva, diventa anche un luogo di produzione e trasformazione, nel quale il lavoro artistico può svilupparsi attraverso gesti ripetuti e tempi non necessariamente coincidenti con quelli della produzione professionale.

Il lavoro di Marisa Merz non segue un’evoluzione lineare

La varietà dei materiali impiegati da Marisa Merz non segue fasi e non procede per liminali separazioni: scultura, installazione, disegno e pittura si incontrano e si sovrappongono, mentre motivi e forme ritornano nel corso degli anni assumendo configurazioni differenti. Le opere possono essere riorganizzate, accostate ad altri elementi o inserite in nuovi contesti, dando origine a relazioni diverse, e anche i materiali più fragili o apparentemente effimeri partecipano a questa logica, valorizzando il modo in cui la forma si costruisce e come può continuare a cambiare.

La sua ricerca è approdata in alcune delle principali mostre internazionali

Nel corso della sua carriera, Marisa Merz ha partecipato a importanti appuntamenti espositivi internazionali e la retrospettiva torinese riparte da questa complessità per proporre una lettura articolata della sua opera. Al Castello di Rivoli, il percorso ruota attorno a E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare , installazione presentata nel 1980 alla galleria Tucci Russo di Torino e riproposta nello stesso anno alla Biennale di Venezia. Alla Fondazione Merz, invece, l’attenzione si concentra sui materiali e sui processi di composizione, mentre alla GAM il percorso si avvicina alla dimensione quotidiana e domestica del lavoro, con la presentazione di Living Sculpture dopo il restauro.

Le tre sedi restituiscono così aspetti differenti di una pratica che non si lascia esaurire in una definizione unica, con una retrospettiva che vuole ripercorrere i passi dell’artista nel corso della sua lunga carriera, mantenendo saldo quel baricentro torinese che continua a fungere da bussola indefessa.

article_text:
F ilmed in Taiwan and set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a preparation for the real world but as a microcosm of society at large. At this elite private institute, pupils studiously march in lines like obedient soldiers, their purple uniforms the only pop of colour in a grey building of glass and steel. The school’s operations have a touch of dystopian sci-fi: students check in with AI recognition panels, which also display their class standing and disciplinary scores. In this sterile environment where human worth is measured by standardised metrics, the breathing room for individuality is nil.

This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

Though grappling with heavy subjects such as self-harm, bullying and drug use, Chow treats these youthful foibles as evidence of a systemic malaise rather than individual failings. A staunch anti-authoritarian message is smuggled in the conventions of a whodunnit thriller; it parallels Chow’s previous films, including the 2021 documentary Revolution of Our Times , about the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests . Like the rebellion in Deadline, that movement also began on campuses and was led by students. That both titles are banned in Hong Kong only underscores the urgency and importance of Chow’s film-making.

article_text:
Ci sono fiere che seguono le categorie e fiere che amano metterle in discussione. BRAFA Art Fair appartiene decisamente alla seconda famiglia: qui un maestro antico può dialogare con un’icona del design, un oggetto d’uso quotidiano trasformarsi in un’opera da collezione e il vetro diventare materia di sperimentazione contemporanea. Da segnare in agenda, portandosi già avanti dopo gli appuntamenti internazionali a New York, nel Golfo e a Miami: da domenica 24 a domenica 31 gennaio 2027, il Brussels Expo ospiterà la 72ª edizione di BRAFA, con 150 gallerie provenienti da 18 Paesi e ben 27 discipline artistiche. Un universo che attraversa archeologia, pittura antica, scultura, fotografia, arti decorative, design, gioielleria, arte africana e asiatica, fino alle più raffinate manifatture di vetro e ceramica.

La parola chiave per il 2027: eclettismo . Una direzione precisa, che passa attraverso nuovi espositori, specializzazioni inedite e una presenza ancora più articolata di arte antica, arti etniche e design. «Sono particolarmente fiero di annunciare un’edizione BRAFA 2027 ancora più ricca e interessante», dichiara Klaas Muller, presidente della manifestazione. Il merito, spiega, è anche di un’attività di scouting che porterà a Bruxelles nuove gallerie di primo piano sulla scena internazionale.

Le gallerie italiane a Brafa 2027: tredici voci, un panorama senza confini

Dagli Old Masters al design del Novecento, dall’Arte Povera al vetro contemporaneo, passando per alta gioielleria, arte africana e asiatica e orologeria vintage, la presenza italiana restituisce un’immagine sfaccettata del collezionismo. Sono tredici le realtà comprese nella selezione fornita per questa edizione, con specializzazioni che attraversano secoli di storia e linguaggi molto diversi. Un racconto che si sviluppa senza compartimenti stagni, proprio come piace a BRAFA.

Sul versante dell’arte antica, Mearini Fine Art , da Perugia, punta a BRAFA 2027 sulla scultura con un capitello corinzio in marmo greco, riconducibile a una variante di un modello romano e databile fra la fine del XII e l’inizio del XIII secolo, accanto a un Apostolo in bassorilievo di Montorsoli del 1550. Due opere che mettono in relazione il mondo medievale e quello rinascimentale, raccontando la continuità e le trasformazioni della tradizione scultorea. Lo sguardo si allarga con Dei Bardi Art , con sede a Bruxelles e specializzata in sculture europee antiche e opere d’arte dei primi secoli, mentre Verdini Antiques , da Roma, costruisce un percorso fra mobili, oggetti, dipinti e sculture. Fra i pezzi annunciati anche un piano circolare con una Medusa, presenza che richiama la persistenza del mito classico nel repertorio delle arti decorative.

La pittura porta il visitatore in un viaggio attraverso le grandi scuole europee. Caretto & Occhinegro , galleria torinese al debutto a BRAFA, si concentra sui maestri fiamminghi, olandesi e tedeschi fra XV e XVII secolo, mentre W. Apolloni-Laocoon Gallery , attiva fra Roma e Londra, attraversa il periodo dal XVII al XIX secolo con dipinti, disegni e sculture. Il Settecento italiano è invece il territorio di Brun Fine Art , presente fra Milano e Firenze, mentre Ars Antiqua , da Milano, affianca agli Old Masters mobili, scultura e arte moderna. Quattro prospettive diverse che, insieme, compongono una lettura articolata della storia artistica europea, fra scuole pittoriche, arti applicate e differenti sensibilità collezionistiche.

Il Novecento cambia ritmo e apre a nuove contaminazioni. Per BRAFA 2027, robertaebasta , realtà milanese con sede anche a Londra e presenza storica della manifestazione, mette in scena un incontro fra tre Concetti spaziali – Teatrino di Lucio Fontana del 1965, la credenza Cityscape di Paul Evans, realizzata intorno al 1970 in acciaio cromato e dorato, e Turf War di Banksy, serigrafia del 2003. Arte, design e cultura visiva contemporanea si ritrovano così sullo stesso palcoscenico, in un accostamento che attraversa generazioni e linguaggi. Su un altro versante della ricerca, Repetto Gallery , con sede a Lugano, segue il filo della materia e del paesaggio attraverso l’arte italiana del secondo dopoguerra, l’Arte Povera e la Land Art: un percorso in cui l’opera si confronta con lo spazio, i materiali e i processi creativi.

Fra le novità da tenere d’occhio c’è poi Galleria Barovier&Toso , storica realtà di Murano, Venezia, che debutta a BRAFA con vetri d’autore e arte contemporanea. La tradizione vetraria veneziana incontra così una sensibilità progettuale aperta alla sperimentazione, confermando come le arti decorative possano essere un terreno di ricerca attuale e non soltanto una testimonianza del passato.

Il collezionismo si sposta quindi verso due universi in cui il dettaglio e la qualità esecutiva hanno un ruolo centrale. Bernardini , fra Milano e Hong Kong, porta in fiera la propria specializzazione nell’orologeria di alta gamma, con il Rolex Oyster Chronograph in oro giallo del 1956 annunciato fra le rarità dell’edizione. Nardi Venezia , invece, rappresenta l’alta gioielleria, aggiungendo al percorso una dimensione in cui preziosità dei materiali, ricerca formale e maestria artigianale diventano protagoniste. A completare il panorama è Dalton Somaré , galleria milanese dedicata all’arte africana e asiatica. Fra le opere annunciate figura una sedia Chokwe proveniente dall’Angola e databile alla fine del XIX secolo. Qui la funzione pratica dell’oggetto si intreccia con il suo valore simbolico e sociale, trasformandolo in un segno di rango e autorità.

Il Musée d’Ixelles torna in scena

Fra le anticipazioni più significative dell’edizione c’è anche l’ospite d’onore: il Musée d’Ixelles, che riaprirà al pubblico nel marzo 2027 dopo dieci anni di importanti lavori di ristrutturazione. Il museo, situato in Rue Jean Van Volsem 71 a Ixelles, conserva e studia oltre 15.000 opere dedicate al patrimonio artistico belga dal XIX secolo a oggi. La partecipazione a BRAFA precede dunque un momento importante per la vita culturale della città e offre l’occasione di riportare l’attenzione su una collezione che si prepara a incontrare nuovamente il pubblico.

«Riaprire significa creare legami: un passato ricco di quasi 135 anni di impegno artistico con un presente in movimento», spiega Claire Leblanc, direttrice-conservatrice del museo. Un messaggio che si accorda perfettamente con lo spirito della fiera: creare connessioni, riattivare storie, avvicinare pubblici e prospettive diverse. Anche il programma dei BRAFA Art Talks contribuirà a questo dialogo. Ad aprire il ciclo di conferenze, nel pomeriggio di sabato 23 gennaio, sarà un intervento del Museo Egizio di Torino. L’appuntamento con BRAFA 2027 è a gennaio, a Bruxelles.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在DC漫画中，“泥面人”是蝙蝠侠的主要敌人之一。但在詹姆斯·瓦特金斯于本周三上映的这部电影中，这位黑暗骑士并未出现，“泥面人”反而成为了一部复仇故事的主角。

article_text:
Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) est un comédien à gueule d’ange à qui tout sourit, quand un malfrat le défigure avec un couteau. Toute sa carrière s’écroule, mais heureusement il trouve une scientifique qui lui injecte des nanocellules qui soudainement réparent ses tissus.

Seulement son visage peut s’affaisser sans prévenir jusqu’à devenir monstrueux. Le joli visage de Matt ressemble alors à une toile grimaçante de Francis Bacon ou à un personnage cronenbergien à vif et couleur chair.

Sa peau fond en fait comme une vieille pâte dès que ses sentiments deviennent trop forts. Peu à peu, l’acteur reprend la maîtrise de ses émotions, et malaxe cette glaise comme bon lui semble, jusqu’à pouvoir incarner qui il veut.

Le film devient alors une version horrifique de The Mask (parfois tout aussi cartoonesque mais beaucoup plus inquiète) dans lequel Matt devient l’acteur ultime, jouant la comédie pour assouvir sa vengeance contre ceux qui l’ont mutilé et contre l’industrie du cinéma qui l’a laissé tomber.

Clayface vise moins les diktats de beauté et de jeunesse auxquels sont soumis les actrices (comme dans The Substance de Coralie Fargeat qui parlait du temps passant sur le visage des interprètes) qu’un milieu du cinéma mis à l’épreuve à l’ère de la post-vérité. Quels masques renvoient les acteurs et actrices aujourd’hui ?

▌ À LIRE AUSSI

Making-of : dans les coulisses du dément The Substance de Coralie Fargeat

Toute interprétation au théâtre ou cinéma est-elle monstrueuse au sens où un.e acteurice fait corps avec son personnage ? Et surtout ne vaut-il pas mieux croire à cet état mutant et très organique de l’incarnation, aussi dangereux soit-il, plutôt qu’aux fausses performances IA qu’on voit de plus en plus tourner ? Toute interprétation au théâtre ou cinéma est-elle monstrueuse au sens où un.e acteurice fait corps avec son personnage ? Et surtout ne vaut-il pas mieux croire à cet état mutant et très organique de l’incarnation, aussi dangereux soit-il, plutôt qu’aux fausses performances IA qu’on voit de plus en plus tourner ?

Clayface anticipe un autre traité de l’acteurice prévu pour la fin de l’année : The Debut de Jesse Eisenberg. Dans cette comédie musicale, le personnage de Julianne Moore en mode actor’s studio va jusqu’au bout de son personnage, jusqu’à peu à peu devenir celui-ci. Les deux films affirment la foi inflexible des interprètes dans leur art. On se plaît nous aussi à continuer d’y croire.

title_original: « Quelques mots d’amour » de Rudi Rosenberg : en quête de tendresse
editorial_title_zh: 吕迪·罗森伯格的《Quelques mots d’amour》：对温柔的追寻
editorial_excerpt_zh: 通过聚焦一个家庭——其中大女儿试图寻找从未谋面的父亲——吕迪·罗森伯格在笑泪交织中成功刻画了萨塞勒那些心地善良的人物对爱的渴望。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/654492a6a2e060b5618af12221946790-1-1024x553.webp", "alt": "654492a6a2e060b5618af12221946790 1", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吕迪·罗森伯格的第二部电影（继2015年上映的《新郎 Vêtements pour garçons》之后，注：根据常识或原文译名保持）以一个具有卸防般简单感的镜头开场。7岁的阿比盖尔陪着母亲埃丽卡（哈夫西娅·赫尔齐饰）按响了一个对讲机。此行的目的是让小女孩终于见到她从未谋面的父亲，但那名男子仅在窗前一闪而过，拒绝开门。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在阿比盖尔眼中，这个父亲的形象因此成了一个模糊的身影，她在随后的岁月中一直试图寻找他。影片故事设定在萨塞勒，时间先是1995年，随后是2000年代初，《Quelques mots d’amour》勾勒了一名单身母亲及其两个孩子（阿比盖尔和她的弟弟约尼）的肖像，这个家庭三人组在一位精妙结合幽默感与极致温柔的电影人珍视的目光下构建起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这里，弟弟无聊的玩笑、少女阿比如胶似漆的友谊，或是母亲在周围人身上寻找理解之耳的笨拙举动，都如同对被爱与被倾听的急切呼唤。随着阿比盖尔（分别由埃拉·贝杜沙和努尔·萨拉姆饰演）长大并开始痴迷于寻找这位未知的父亲，她冷落了家里的其他人，没有察觉到身边所有的情感宝藏。而吕迪·罗森伯格的才华恰恰在于，他通过悲喜交加的笔触，让人感受到这群人物身上无与伦比的慷慨。他们让2000年代的萨塞勒吹拂起一股快乐共处之风，其中那些历经许久才得以表达并找到出路的灿烂爱意最终绽放出光芒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吕迪·罗森伯格的《Quelques mots d’amour》，10月28日上映，Ad Vitam（1小时37分钟）", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关注我们", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Le deuxième film de Rudi Rosenberg (après Le Nouveau, sorti en 2015) débute par une séquence à la simplicité désarmante. Abigaëlle, 7 ans, accompagne sa mère Erika (Hafsia Herzi) qui sonne à un interphone. L’objectif est que la petite fille rencontre enfin son père, qu’elle n’a jamais connu, mais l’homme n’apparaît que furtivement à la fenêtre et refuse d’ouvrir.

Cette figure paternelle demeure ainsi aux yeux d’Abigaëlle une silhouette floue qu’elle cherchera à retrouver au fil des ans. Situé à Sarcelles, d’abord en 1995 puis au début des années 2000, Quelques mots d’amour dresse le portrait d’une mère célibataire et de ses deux enfants (Abigaëlle et son petit frère Yoni), trio familial qui se construit sous le précieux regarde d’un cinéaste alliant brillamment sens de l’humour et tendresse absolue.

Ici, les blagues vaseuses du petit frère, les amitiés fusionnelles de l’adolescente Abi ou les maladresses d’une mère qui cherche auprès de son entourage des oreilles compréhensives sonnent comme autant de besoins criants d’être aimé et entendu. À mesure qu’Abigaëlle (tour à tour interprétée par Ella Bedoucha et Nour Salam) grandit et devient obsédée par la quête de ce père inconnu, elle délaisse le reste de sa famille et ne décèle pas tous les trésors affectifs qu’elle a autour d’elle. Et le talent de Rudi Rosenberg consiste justement à faire ressentir, par touches tragi-comiques, la générosité extrême d’une communauté de personnages. Ils font souffler sur le Sarcelles des années 2000 un vent de cohabitation joyeuse, où finissent par irradier de splendides preuves d’amour qui ont mis longtemps à s’exprimer et trouver leur chemin.

Quelques mots d’amour de Rudi Rosenberg, sortie le 28 octobre, Ad Vitam (1 h 37)

excerpt_original: En s’intéressant à une famille, dont la fille aînée cherche à retrouver son père qu’elle n’a jamais connu, Rudi Rosenberg réussit à dépeindre, entre rires et larmes, le besoin d’amour de personnages sarcellois au grand cœur.

editorial_title_zh: 档案：摄影艺术基金会：摆好姿势！自动照相亭诞生100周年
editorial_excerpt_zh: 档案 – 2025年10月22日今年秋天，摄影艺术基金会（The Photographers’ Gallery）迎来备受喜爱的自动照相亭诞生100周年。通过特别的档案展览，“摆好 […] Cet article Archives : The Photographers’ Gallery : Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth est apparu en…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "档案 – 2025年10月22日", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年秋天，摄影艺术基金会（The Photographers’ Gallery）迎来备受喜爱的自动照相亭诞生100周年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过特别的档案展览，“摆好姿势！自动照相亭诞生100周年”（Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth）回顾了自动照相亭的历史，并探讨了其私密迷人的魅力、不完美之处以及独特性格。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025年标志着阿纳托尔·约瑟夫（Anatol Josepho）发明模拟自动照相亭100周年的全年庆祝活动。他的第一台 Photomaton 于1925年在纽约百老汇问世。自动照相亭彻底改变了摄影世界，并迅速成为世界各地城市中随处可见的风景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为集照相馆和冲印实验室于一体的设施，照相亭首次让人能以实惠的价格接触摄影。无需任何技术知识，也无需操作员，任何人都可以走进布帘后面，把钱投入投币口，摆好姿势。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在第一台照相亭获得成功后——在前5天里有超过7,500名纽约人使用——全球范围内的成功也随之而来。英国的第一台自动照相亭于1928年在伦敦塞尔福里奇百货公司（Selfridges）推出，并立即大获成功。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在1950年代和1960年代，自动照相亭是集市、购物中心和火车站的常见设施。这些私密且便宜的空间让每个人都拥有控制自己影像的自由。在布帘后，无论是独自一人还是和朋友挤在一起，自动照相亭都是一个远离摄影师视线的游乐场。从约翰·列农（John Lennon）和小野洋子（Yoko Ono），到约翰和杰奎琳·肯尼迪（John and Jacqueline Kennedy），人人都喜爱照相亭，艺术家安迪·沃霍尔（Andy Warhol）也曾用它来创作著名的自画像系列。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些曾遍布商业街和车站的投币式照相亭，随着1990年代数字摄影的兴起而消失了。如今，经过热心专家的修复，模拟照相亭正重新出现在世界各地的城市中，并受到现代粉丝的重新关注和喜爱。除了展示档案照片、复古照片条和材料外，画廊内还将设立一个照相亭，供大家创作自己的自拍纪念品，并提供现场直播，展示照相亭独特的运作机械。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“摆好姿势！自动照相亭诞生100周年”（Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth）展出了雷纳尔·佩利西耶（Raynal Pellicer）收藏的作品，是与 AUTOFOTO 合作开展的百年庆典全年活动的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摆好姿势！自动照相亭诞生100周年 2025年10月10日 – 2026年2月22日 摄影艺术基金会（The Photographers’ Gallery） 伦敦拉米利街16-18号 W1F 7LW www.tpg.org.uk", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Archives – October 22, 2025"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This autumn The Photographers’ Gallery celebrates 100 years of the much-loved photobooth."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Through a special archival display, Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth looks back on the history of the photobooth and explores its intimate charms, imperfections and quirks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025 marks the year-long celebration of the 100th anniversary of the invention of the analogue photobooth by Anatol Josepho. His first Photomaton appeared on Broadway in New York in 1925. The photobooth was a game-changer for the world of photography and quickly became an everyday sight in cities around the world."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A combined studio and photography lab in one place, booths offered the first affordable access to photography. With no technical knowledge needed and no operator, anyone could step behind the curtain, put their money in the slot and strike a pose."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After the success of the first booth, when over 7,500 New Yorkers used the booth in its first 5 days, global success quickly followed. The first photobooth launched in the UK in Selfridges, London, in 1928 and was an immediate hit."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the 1950s and 1960s, photobooths were a common feature at fairs, shopping centres and train stations. article_text:
Archives – October 22, 2025

This autumn The Photographers’ Gallery celebrates 100 years of the much-loved photobooth.

Through a special archival display, Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth looks back on the history of the photobooth and explores its intimate charms, imperfections and quirks.

2025 marks the year-long celebration of the 100th anniversary of the invention of the analogue photobooth by Anatol Josepho. His first Photomaton appeared on Broadway in New York in 1925. The photobooth was a game-changer for the world of photography and quickly became an everyday sight in cities around the world.

A combined studio and photography lab in one place, booths offered the first affordable access to photography. With no technical knowledge needed and no operator, anyone could step behind the curtain, put their money in the slot and strike a pose.

After the success of the first booth, when over 7,500 New Yorkers used the booth in its first 5 days, global success quickly followed. The first photobooth launched in the UK in Selfridges, London, in 1928 and was an immediate hit.

In the 1950s and 1960s, photobooths were a common feature at fairs, shopping centres and train stations. These intimate inexpensive spaces gave everyone the freedom to control their own images. Behind the curtain, whether alone or crammed in with friends, the photobooth was a playground, beyond the gaze of a photographer. The booths were loved by everyone, from John Lennon and Yoko Ono, to John and Jacqueline Kennedy, and used by artist Andy Warhol for his famous series of self-portraits.

The coin-operated booths, once ever-present on high streets and stations, disappeared with the rise of digital photography in the 1990s. Now, restored by dedicated experts, analogue booths are reappearing in cities across the world and enjoying a resurgence of interest and delight with modern-day fans. Alongside the display of archive prints, vintage strips and materials, there’ll also be a booth at the Gallery for everyone to create their own selfie souvenir and a live feed to see the unique mechanics of the booth in action.

Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth features work from the collection of Raynal Pellicer and is part of a year-long programme of centenary celebrations, in partnership with AUTOFOTO.

Strike a Pose! 100 Years of the Photobooth 10 October 2025 – 22 February 2026 The Photographers’ Gallery 16–18 Ramillies Street London W1F 7LW www.tpg.org.uk

Lopez Cassell）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布兰妮·夏恩（Brittany Shyne）的《种子》（Seeds）以惊人的单色呈现，充满了美国南部黑人农耕生活的质感，当它在2025年圣丹斯电影节首映并荣获美国纪录片评审团大奖时，它宣告了创意非虚构电影领域一个非凡的新声音。这部最初作为夏恩艺术硕士（MFA）毕业论文的项目，经过九年倾注心血的打磨，成长为一部由关注与信任塑造的电影。《种子》开篇于一位黑人长者的葬礼，随后跟随几代人在佐治亚州和密西西比州土地上耕作的世纪农民，他们为保护承载着其历史的土地免遭种族经济剥夺而战。夏恩的方法是极度独立的——她独自从俄亥俄州开车到底格里斯河谷/美国深南部（Deep South），并亲自完成了摄影和录音——这赋予了这部电影非凡的亲密感。她的孤独为其首部剧情长片注入了一种安静的抒情性。通过尊重农民们邀请她走入他们生活的契机，夏恩精心打造了一个爱与劳动的时光胶囊，证明了他们曾在这里，且这片土地铭记这一切。——鲁恩·努尔（Ruun Nuur)", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在西班牙电影大年里，加布里埃尔·阿索林（Gabriel Azorín）的长片小说首作《昨晚我征服了底比斯》（Last Night I Conquered the City of Thebes）是一部意料之外的局外人之作。除了包含一个惊艳航拍镜头的漫长开场外，影片完全发生加利西亚的一处古罗马帝国时期的温泉中，一群似乎刚从战争前线归来的年轻人在那里度过了一个夜晚。当男孩们潜入具有修复之力的水中时，所发生的一切既细腻又引人深思。躯体在水中共同浮沉，思绪在时间的池水中浸润，双眼适应着黑暗，新的维度随之开启。阿索林这部兼具致敬与超越爱德华多·威廉姆斯（Eduardo Williams）、阿彼察pong·韦拉斯哈古（Apichatpong Weerasethakul）以及阿尔伯特·塞拉（Albert Serra）等电影人当代策略的杰作，是一场穿梭于星辰、废墟、历史战役与虚拟战争的迷幻之旅，探索了转瞬即逝却又永恒、既是线性又是循环的梦幻般的电影时间。——安托万·蒂里翁（Antoine Thirion）", "translated": true}]

(Of course, that could change at any moment; keep an eye on FC for future coverage!)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For the best films that received a theatrical or streaming release in the U.S. this year, go to the Best Films of 2025 list."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Curious to see who voted and for which films? Read our voters’ individual ballots . Also, don’t miss our Best of 2025 Countdown Podcast , featuring guest critics Amy Taubin and Bilge Ebiri."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Also, read critic and programmer Inney Prakash’s list of the year’s Best Short Films , filmmaker and programmer Gina Telaroli’s list of the Best Restorations , critic and editor Gavin Smith’s list of the year’s Best Repertory Releases , and writing on the Best Scenes by Devika Girish and the Best Performances by Michael Koresky, all available in the links above."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kamal Aljafari’s quiet and haunting With Hasan in Gaza , made from MiniDV tapes shot in 2001, returns us to a Gaza still standing and accessible to the Palestinian filmmaker more than 20 years ago. Documenting Aljafari’s search for a friend with whom he shared a prison cell as a teenager, the film is composed entirely of this “found” footage, minimally framed in the present by captions relaying his prison memories and a soundtrack that alternates a sparse synth score with brilliantly selected Palestinian and Arab songs, whose lyrics recast the images in light of Gaza’s destruction. Much of With Hasan ’s pathos lies in our anachronistic encounter with Gaza’s once-vibrant streets and souks, where smiling children play and fresh vegetables abound. Rarely in cinema is Gaza granted the care of close, tender observation that seeks to know the place from the perspective of a neighbor and friend rather than a journalist or emergency worker.— Kareem Estefan"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Lucrecia Martel, time is of the essence—in particular, what she calls the “conventional straight arrow version, like a ray of light,” which hurtles past both history and the present in the name of progress. Her feature doc debut starts with the 2009 killing of an Indigenous activist by police and landowners trying to evict the Chuschagasta community from their ancestral lands. article_text:
Our Best Undistributed Films list, voted on by Film Comment contributors worldwide, recognizes the new films that premiered—at festivals, or elsewhere—in 2025 but did not have U.S. distribution at press time. (Of course, that could change at any moment; keep an eye on FC for future coverage!)

For the best films that received a theatrical or streaming release in the U.S. this year, go to the Best Films of 2025 list.

Curious to see who voted and for which films? Read our voters’ individual ballots . Also, don’t miss our Best of 2025 Countdown Podcast , featuring guest critics Amy Taubin and Bilge Ebiri.

Also, read critic and programmer Inney Prakash’s list of the year’s Best Short Films , filmmaker and programmer Gina Telaroli’s list of the Best Restorations , critic and editor Gavin Smith’s list of the year’s Best Repertory Releases , and writing on the Best Scenes by Devika Girish and the Best Performances by Michael Koresky, all available in the links above.

Kamal Aljafari’s quiet and haunting With Hasan in Gaza , made from MiniDV tapes shot in 2001, returns us to a Gaza still standing and accessible to the Palestinian filmmaker more than 20 years ago. Documenting Aljafari’s search for a friend with whom he shared a prison cell as a teenager, the film is composed entirely of this “found” footage, minimally framed in the present by captions relaying his prison memories and a soundtrack that alternates a sparse synth score with brilliantly selected Palestinian and Arab songs, whose lyrics recast the images in light of Gaza’s destruction. Much of With Hasan ’s pathos lies in our anachronistic encounter with Gaza’s once-vibrant streets and souks, where smiling children play and fresh vegetables abound. Rarely in cinema is Gaza granted the care of close, tender observation that seeks to know the place from the perspective of a neighbor and friend rather than a journalist or emergency worker.— Kareem Estefan

For Lucrecia Martel, time is of the essence—in particular, what she calls the “conventional straight arrow version, like a ray of light,” which hurtles past both history and the present in the name of progress. Her feature doc debut starts with the 2009 killing of an Indigenous activist by police and landowners trying to evict the Chuschagasta community from their ancestral lands. But the film treats this incident not as an exceptional rupture—a point on a line—as the judicial system makes it out to be. Her approach is centrifugal, spinning out from footage of the shooting and the ensuing hearings to extensive research into the thefts and sleights of legal hand that have, over centuries, turned bureaucracy into a weapon of the slow, ongoing, and entirely sanctioned murder of Indigenous life. In a visual corollary, occasional drone shots pull us out of the present, evoking the ghostly feeling that the land precedes all the rigmarole we see onscreen—that it stood witness to lives that came before even the state of Argentina.— Devika Girish

Since Ross McElwee’s 1985 breakthrough Sherman’s March , the filmmaker’s first-person documentaries have used his life as raw material. But the material has never been as raw as in his new film, Remake . We learn early on that McElwee’s son, Adrian, died of a drug overdose in 2016, at 27 years of age; the film is a deep dive through past and present to sort through the lives of father and son. The title was inspired by a misbegotten Hollywood attempt to remake Sherman’s March as a fiction feature, but it also comes to signal many other things over the course of the film: parents’ attempts to remake themselves through their children; how a remarriage is a remake of a failed union; and the ways in which cinema attempts to remake life. In the film’s opening scenes, McElwee asks a 7-year-old Adrian what he loves about fishing. His response also applies to Ross’s filmmaking: “The deep surprise of the ocean. You never know what you’ll catch.”— David Schwartz

The second feature by Canadian filmmaker Rhayne Vermette is a cryptic nocturne set in Ste. Anne, Manitoba, where the outdoors is all darkness and whipping snow, and interiors are lit by the silvery static of old television sets. A strange monolith appears. A civil servant pursues an investigation, viewing security-camera footage and reading through files relating to the commissioning of a monument. Its sculptor, an elderly woman, grieves someone’s death. Nuns perform a sinister ceremony, collecting the tears of an Indigenous woman and bottling them as holy water. A man leads a procession to a graveyard, holding up an infinity symbol, which is also the symbol of the Métis Nation, to which Vermette belongs. The film’s poetic symbology—moon, mirror, stone, river—is embedded in a laconic depiction of everyday life; its runic images, captured on broken Bolex cameras, stay etched in the mind, perhaps all the more so for being unexplained.— Imogen Sara Smith

Pedro Pinho’s three-and-a-half-hour epic is an open world through which the viewer is encouraged to wander freely. Portuguese civil engineer Sérgio (Sérgio Coragem) arrives in Guinea-Bissau to conduct an environmental-impact study for a proposed road, continuing the work of an Italian predecessor who abandoned the project under mysterious circumstances. A feckless naïf who leaves roadkill in a communal fridge, Sérgio generates awkward comic friction wherever he goes: to Bissau’s nightclubs; to villages performing traditional rituals for back-patting aid workers in matching T-shirts; to an energy plant in the desert and the brothel where its European contractors blow off steam. I Only Rest in the Storm ’s caustic thesis, about the legacy of colonial violence that persists in the development agenda, emerges from scenes of labor, partying, and explicit sex that Pinho, a former documentarian, stages with a verité density.— Mark Asch

It’s not the only 2025 release about aging revolutionaries, but Escape comes to us from a filmmaker uniquely equipped to speak to the subject: Masao Adachi, now 86 years old, left the heyday of the Japanese New Wave in 1971 to co-direct a documentary with the Japanese Red Army in Lebanon, then dedicated himself to Palestinian liberation until he was extradited to Japan in 2000. His latest is a biopic of anarchist Satoshi Kirishima, who evaded capture for nearly 50 years after participating in a series of bombings against Japanese corporations in the mid-’70s—until, remarkably, he revealed his true identity on his deathbed in 2024. Adachi has characterized Kirishima’s lonely life on the run as “a form of struggle,” which the film renders in quiet, quotidian detail. Memories of the comrades Kirishima has lost crossfade into his present, accumulating a half century of reenactments and apparitions. Painful as they are, these recollections compel him to keep their struggle alive—and devotion to their cause, Adachi suggests, is a marathon, not a sprint.— Chloe Lizotte

Pin de fartie is not so much an adaptation as an anagram of Samuel Beckett’s Fin de partie , or Endgame . Alejo Moguillansky—a member of the whimsical, genre-bending Argentine troupe El Pampero Cine—expands the one-act play into multiple nested narratives organized around three contrapuntal pairs, each approaching a parting of ways. A despotic blind father (Santiago Gobernori) aggravates his servant-like daughter (Cleo Moguillansky) in a bucolic Swiss canton; two actors (Laura Paredes and Marcos Ferrante) nurture a latent desire for one another while rehearsing Fin de partie in Buenos Aires; a blind, aging pianist (Margarita Fernández) and her son (Moguillansky himself) discover the uncanny similarities between themselves and the characters in Beckett’s play. It would all be too twee if not for Moguillansky’s fourth-wall-breaking games, revealing the props, the foley artists, and the presence of two omniscient narrators. Each repetition brings the duos closer to their inevitable separations, which are constantly deferred by Moguillansky’s hopelessly romantic impulse to hold on—if only for one more act.— Cici Peng

Halfway through Bouchra , our titular protagonist encounters a classic lesbian conundrum: “I didn’t know if she was flirting or if I was just, like, making it up.” It doesn’t help that Bouchra, a New York–based artist originally from Morocco, is visiting her hometown of Casablanca. The longings and complexities of the diasporic life add to her confusion, as does the fact that she’s at a crossroads with both work and a family unable to contend with her queerness. Directed by artist-filmmakers Meriem Bennani and Orian Barki (of the viral web series 2 Lizards ), this animated feature is a witty, tender wonder of a film, partly based on Bennani’s own life. The characters are represented by anthropomorphic animals (our heroine is a lithe, stylish coyote), and yet Bouchra feels astonishingly visceral, rendering a recognizably moody New York and a vibrant, jewel-toned Casablanca with CGI, and incorporating real-life conversations (including phone calls between Bennani and her mother). The result is an intimate meditation on the porous boundaries between life and art.— Dessane Lopez Cassell

Rendered in striking monochrome and alive to the textures of Black agrarian life in the American South, Brittany Shyne’s Seeds announced an extraordinary new voice in creative nonfiction cinema when it premiered at Sundance 2025 and won the U.S. Documentary Grand Jury Prize. What began as Shyne’s MFA thesis grew, across nine devoted years, into a film shaped by attention and trust. Seeds opens with the funeral of a Black elder, and then follows centennial farmers whose families have tended Georgia and Mississippi soil for generations as they fight to protect the land that holds their history from racio-economic dispossession. Shyne’s approach was hyper-independent—she drove down alone from Ohio to the Deep South and did her own cinematography and sound recording—and that gives the film its remarkable intimacy. Her solitude breathes a quiet lyricism into her debut feature. Honoring the farmers’ invitation into their lives, Shyne crafts a time capsule of love and labor, proof that they were here and that the land remembers.— Ruun Nuur

In a great year for Spanish cinema, Gabriel Azorín’s debut fiction feature, Last Night I Conquered the City of Thebes , is the unexpected outsider. Except for a lengthy opening sequence containing one stunning drone shot, the film exclusively takes place in a Roman Empire–era hot springs in Galicia, where a group of young men who appear to have returned from the front lines of a war spend the night. What happens as the boys plunge into the regenerative waters is both delicate and thought-provoking. Bodies float together, minds soak in pools of time, eyes adjust to darkness, and new dimensions open. Evoking—and expanding beyond—the contemporary strategies of filmmakers like Eduardo Williams, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, and Albert Serra, Azorín’s tour de force is a trippy journey through stars and ruins and historical battles and virtual wars, exploring cinematic time as a dream both fleeting and permanent, simultaneously linear and circular.— Antoine Thirion

article_text:
“You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ‘s phenomenally successful documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, swept the Critics Choice Association ‘s documentary awards tonight, winning each of its five categories — including Best Documentary Feature. Ava DuVernay’s “14th,” which headed into the night with the most nominations (six), went home empty-handed.

In addition to the top prize, “You Can See Everything” won Best Director (Fielder and Oppenheimer), Best Cinematography (David Bolen), Best Editing (Adam Locke-Norton), and Best Music Score (Ari Balouzian).

Whether or not this is a harbinger of the film ‘s Oscar chances is anybody’s guess. A24 is aggressively campaigning for “You Can See Everything” to score both Best Documentary and Best Picture nominations. If the film receives the latter, it would be the first documentary ever to do so. The CCA sweep certainly doesn’t hurt its prospects, but it’s not necessarily a predictor either — in the last 10 years, the CCA and Academy have only agreed on the best documentary twice (with “O.J.: Made in America” and “Summer of Soul”).

Other winners tonight included David Greaves’ “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” which took home awards for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Historical Documentary and Best Archival Documentary, and Alex Gibney’s four-hour “Musk,” which won Best Biographical Documentary. John Wilson scored an award for Best Narration for his work as writer and performer on “A History of Concrete,” and Baz Luhrmann’s maximalist “EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert” won Best Music Documentary.

The movie currently favored by many awards season pundits to take home the Best Documentary Oscar, “Naza,” won Best Political Documentary, and Best Science/Nature Documentary went to “Nuisance Bear.” Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s widely acclaimed “Everest: The Other Side” was awarded Best Sports Documentary.

BEST DOCUMENTARY FEATURE

“You Can See Everything” (A24)

BEST DIRECTOR

Nathan Fielder & Lance Oppenheim – “You Can See Everything” (A24)

BEST FIRST DOCUMENTARY FEATURE

David Greaves – “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (Neon)

BEST CINEMATOGRAPHY

David Bolen – “You Can See Everything” (A24)

BEST EDITING

Adam Locke-Norton – “You Can See Everything” (A24)

BEST NARRATION

“The History of Concrete” (Magnolia Pictures) Written and Performed by John Wilson

BEST SCORE

Ari Balouzian – “You Can See Everything” (A24)

BEST MUSIC DOCUMENTARY

article_text:
International distributors continue to fall for “ Ulya .”

The Latvian Oscar submission for Best International Feature Film has closed North America (New Mountain Films), France (Destiny), Italy (Invisible Carpet), Slovakia (ASFK), former Yugoslavia (Five Star Distribution), Estonia (Hea Film), Lithuania (GPI), MENA (Teleview), Finland (Cinema Orion), Poland (1989) and Brazil (Belas Arte).

The black-and-white film, directed by Viesturs Kairišs , will open the 30th edition of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . It premiered at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section. Produced by Ego Media (LV), Allfilm (EE), Staroń Film (PL) and Tremora (LT), it’s sold by B-Rated International.

Inspired by the life of legendary basketball player Ulyana Semjonova, born in 1952, “Ulya” is not a typical biopic.

“I don’t think I could ever make a nice, typical biopic. My interest lies in arthouse films. I wasn’t really thinking about sports either. I wanted to tell a Werner Herzog-esque story about a giant girl living in the countryside,” Kairišs told Variety .

Semjonova was known for her size; she stood at seven feet tall. But it also made her a bit of a recluse.

“I’ve been wondering how to get into her head. I wanted it to be very, very subjective. To stick to her point of view, we used what we called ‘crazy cameras’ and slightly out-of-focus shots. Finding the landscape of her inner soul was a very concrete task.”

It was not Kairišs who came up with the idea of making a film about Semjonova. It was the long-held dream of his lead, Kārlis Arnolds Avots .

“When I became the artistic director of the Dailes Theatre, I was looking for actors and he was outstanding. During our first meeting, when I asked him to join our ensemble, he said: ‘You know, I would like to play Ulyana Semjonova.’ Then I forgot all about it,” recalled Kairišs.

“In theatre, it’s not unusual for men to play women. It goes back to Shakespearean times. A few years later, he played in my film ‘January’. At one point, while I was resting, I heard Kārlis talking to our DP, explaining this idea to him again. That’s when I realized: It’s a film!”

Other collaborators still needed convincing, though. “Everyone wanted us to make a standard biopic. I understand it. It could be a good film, but it wouldn’t be my film. We set out to make a film about a girl and we just had to believe in it.”

As proved by a photograph of Semjonova with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, added at the end of the film, she actually gave them her blessing. She passed away in January, 2026.

“She trusted us. It must have been strange to have us come over and say: ‘And a boy will be playing you.’ But it quickly became clear why it made sense,” said Kairišs.

“I actually saw Kārlis yesterday. He’s been filming [the Viking series] ‘Bloodaxe,’ so he has a long beard and he’s really big right now. But he always felt close to her somehow. He knew how it felt to be treated as a ‘giant’.”

Or simply as an outsider. To Kairišs’ surprise, “Ulya” has managed to connect with all kinds of viewers, regardless of their size. “Everyone is struggling with something they want to hide, but it’s probably the best part of who they are,” he said.

“We had incredible reactions everywhere in Latvia. This film is a blockbuster – we’re already the second most-watched film in history. It was the same at Cannes, Rome and Los Angeles. None of my previous films have received this kind of response. Even my daughter said to me: ‘It’s about me, too.’ We touched upon something that’s very modern and very universal.”

Kairišs added: “There’s so much pressure today to look the same and like the same things. We live in times that try to kill all the difference. Everyone struggles with their identity or feels like a ‘freak’. We just have to learn to trust this freak and embrace it as the best thing about us, rather than trying to get rid of it.”

article_text:
Women-led stories are in short supply on television, according to a new report from data company Luminate .

Shows that centered on women accounted for just 11% of premieres from the beginning of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026 despite drawing 17% of U.S. minutes streamed, per the analysis. That may seem a small gap between supply and demand, but Luminate says that this data “shows women-centered series command more viewing time than the volume of these shows would suggest.”

Related Stories

The Summer 50-Something Female Friendships Took Over Streaming With ‘Five Star Weekend’ & ‘Ride Or Die’s Surprise Success

Prime Video Teases Summer Slate Of YA Originals, Book Adaptations & More From ‘The Love Hypothesis’ To ‘Clashing Through The Snow’

In particular, serialized dramas about women are undersupplied. The subcategory, which includes titles like Hulu’s The Handmaid’s Tale and Furious or Showtime’s Yellowjackets , accounted for one-third of women-centered stories released over much of the last two years but 44% of minutes streamed for such shows.

Luminate postures that the “significant unfulfilled demand” for women-led dramas on television should come as no surprise, given the buzz that they make when they do make it to air. Last year, The Handmaid’s Tale was the most-streamed title on Hulu as it concluded its six-season run. Even more recent, the Emmy Rossum-starrer Furious grew its audience 90% in just five weeks post-premiere, Disney said in September.

Watch on Deadline

Not every category or genre is lacking in women-centered stories, though. For example, Luminate finds the supply of women-led documentaries and foreign language films to be oversaturated in the U.S. market. Meanwhile, thrillers and, surprisingly, literary adaptations are still being undersupplied.

There is a 16-point disparity for literary adaptations, which accounted for nearly a third of minutes streamed among women-led stories but just 16% of supply, Luminate’s report finds.

Naturally, some heavy hitting outliers like Bridgerton and The Handmaid’s Tale contribute to that skew, but still this suggests that there’s plenty of room for more in the space. Streamers have clearly taken note of the demand and are already becoming more bullish, particularly with women-led literary adaptations. After the successes of The Summer I Turned Pretty and Off Campus , Prime Video has developed a whole slate of upcoming women-centered adaptations from Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing to Elsie Silver’s Rose Hill.

Luminate also notes Netflix’s recent adaptation of John Steinbeck’s East of Eden , which has been among the most-watched weekly television titles on Netflix since it premiered.

RELATED: ‘East Of Eden’ Tops Netflix Charts With Soft Opening

“In a TV landscape where female-led dramas are still rare enough to be remarked upon, there is clearly a healthy appetite for them among audiences,” the report reads.

article_text:
Alana Mayo has been promoted to join Julie Rapaport as head of film, production & development at Amazon MGM Studios .

Rapaport and Mayo will report to Courtenay Valenti, the studio’s head of film, streaming and theatrical, who announced the executive moves on Tuesday.

“Our output now spans more than 30 films a year across theatrical and streaming — growth that reflects the trust our studio has built with the creative community and the extraordinary work of our team,” Valenti said in a memo to staff. “To match that scale and drive even greater creative output, I am pleased to announce that Julie Rapaport and Alana Mayo will each serve as Head of Film, Production & Development, reporting to me.”

Related Stories

'KPop Demon Hunters,' 'Squid Game' Stars Fete Netflix's Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases 'Tantara,' 'All of Us Are Dead' Season 2

Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: 'I Know That We Could Do Better'

Rapaport and Mayo will each oversee approximately half the film slate — roughly 15 titles per year spanning all genres across theatrical and streaming.

Rapaport joined Amazon MGM Studios in 2015 and was named head of movies in 2022. “Over the past decade, she has shaped a slate that includes ‘Road House,’ ‘Saltburn,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and ‘Verity’ — cultivating a pipeline that consistently attracts top talent and bold material,” Valenti wrote. “Her creative instincts are exceptional, and the trust she has earned across the creative community is a testament to her leadership.”

Mayo will continue leading Orion Pictures, which she has overseen since 2020. Valenti praised Mayo for cultivating a “legacy of bold, distinctive filmmaking” at the label, with acclaimed films like the Oscar-winning “Women Talking” and “American Fiction,” Oscar-nominated “Nickel Boys,” “Bottoms,” Nia DaCosta’s provocative, modern reimagining of Ibsen’s classic play, “Hedda,” and this year’s “Is God Is” and “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”

“Alana has a gift for identifying and elevating bold, distinctive voices, and the relationships she has built with the talent she champions reflect the kind of creative partnership this studio stands for,” Valenti said.

While Rapaport and Mayo will oversee separate titles, Valenti clarified that “we are not creating separate pods or siloed teams as our senior production & development team members will all work with both Julie and Alana across the entire slate, regardless of specific reporting lines.”

As such, both Rapaport and Mayo will “partner closely with marketing, content strategy, finance, public relations, theatrical distribution and Prime Video programming to align creative, business, and financial decisions across the film team.” Physical production, business affairs, casting, consumer insights, studio operations, music and worldwide theatrical distribution will report to Valenti, alongside Rapaport and Mayo.

The mission, Valenti noted, is to “remain one unified creative team, committed to the storytelling and creative partnerships that define this studio.”

Lichamelijke tekortkomingen omkeren en naar hun hand te zetten, getuigen van hun onmogelijke werkelijkheid. Dat doen de kunstenaars die Mira Thompson voor Mister Motley voor het voetlicht bracht binnen haar reeks Land zonder grenzen. Vandaag sluit ze de serie af met een essay waarin ze Karin Spaink, JJJJJerome Ellis, Lizzy Rose en Melvin Moti uitlicht en misschien ook wel bedankt. ‘ Zij laten op eigen wijze zien dat het lichaam meer is dan een fysieke entiteit. Wanneer onbekommerd functioneren geen automatische vanzelfsprekendheid is, openen zich luikjes die door ervaring en gebrek ingegeven zijn.’
