Wanneer we plaatsnemen, zie ik het pas: aan de tafel naast mij en bevriende collega C. zit een geroemde toneelcoryfee. De toneelcoryfee schuift inschikkelijk haar tas opzij wanneer ze ziet dat ook wij het kleine beetje schaduw willen benutten, plaatsmakend voor mijn weinig soepel bewegende elektrische metgezel. Een gemotoriseerde rolstoel lijdt net zo goed onder de hoge temperaturen.

Bevriende collega C., die zo’n twee keer mijn leeftijd telt, kent onze terrasbuurvrouw uit de wandelgangen van het theater, neemt knipogend plaats tegenover mij, en legt een tentoonstellingsfolder onder mijn neus: ‘Kijk, deze nam ik voor je mee uit London. Op de expositie was alleen kunst te zien van kunstenaars met een chronische ziekte of handicap’. C. is net terug in Nederland en begint geestdriftig te vertellen over de inhoud van de folder.

Het lichtblauwe boekje, eenvoudig van design, bevat geen beeldend materiaal, maar beschrijvingen die de kunstwerken van achtergrondinformatie voorzien. Anders dan objectlabels in musea, zijn hier visuele descripties toegevoegd. In minutieus detail krijgt de lezer mee wat er te zien is. Een noodzakelijkheid voor bezoekers met een visuele beperking, maar ook geïnteresseerden op afstand plukken hiervan de vruchten.

C. zegt iets over een walvis in de tentoonstelling. ‘Excuus, ik ben wat afgeleid vanwege de drukte,’ hoor ik mezelf antwoorden, maar ik weet dat ik de schuld aan het afschuiven ben. De werkelijke aanleiding van mijn afwezige aanwezigheid schuilt in de blauwe papieren die voor mij op tafel liggen en mijn gedachten een andere richting opstuwen.

Eerder die dag viel mijn oog op een door mij meermaals gelezen titel in mijn boekenkast, De vallende vrouw: autobiografie van een lichaam , geschreven door de onlangs overleden publicist, schrijver en redacteur Karin Spaink. Voor Mister Motley liet ze zich niet lang voor haar zelfverkozen einde door mij interviewen . We spraken over haar glansrol in het Cantaballet, vergankelijkheid en hoe een lichaam een politiek doel kan dienen.

Zowel in haar werk als in haar persoonlijke leven wist zij haar lichamelijke tekortkomingen steeds opnieuw om te keren en naar haar hand te zetten. Vlijmscherp onderving Spaink waar redenaties rammelden, hoe een gebrekkig gestel een metafoor kan zijn voor maatschappijkritiek, hoe haar steeds fluctuerende gezondheid haar leven weliswaar sterk beïnvloedde, maar ook vormgaf, soms zelfs kleur bracht.

De scheppende macht van de kunstenaar die met een onmogelijke werkelijkheid te maken heeft: de folder die voor me ligt doet me aan Karin denken.

Terwijl C. een wc-bezoek brengt, maak ik van de gelegenheid gebruik. De tentoonstelling Flare-Up , in Goldsmiths Centre for Contemporary Art London brengt kunstenaars samen “wiens werk zich verhoudt tot de poëtica en esthetiek van ziekte, beperking, neurodivergentie en doofheid. De tentoonstelling, die werk van negentien kunstenaars in Goldsmiths CCA presenteert, brengt beeldhouwkunst, installaties, schilderkunst, film, poëzie, muziek en performance samen als middelen voor expressie en activisme.”

Ik lees een beschrijving van het kunstwerk The Clearing (2022) . De stotterende multidisciplinaire kunstenaar JJJJJerome Ellis verheft taal tot visuele en auditieve kunst. Dysfluent Water , begint de partituur.

Door Ellis’ “ dysfluent “ , manier van uitdrukken, wordt er een eigen idioom geproduceerd. Een van pauzes, witregels, gefragmenteerd gevormde zinnen en letters die dwars over elkaar heen tuimelen. De in de tentoonstelling opgenomen partituur kan tevens gelezen worden als politiek pamflet: Ellis’ werk bevat historische, politieke en Bijbelse verwijzingen en thematiseert de koloniale connotaties van taal en slavernij

Bij thuiskomst kruip ik achter mijn laptop en bestudeer ik de partituur:

“They called us river folk

cuz’ we met on the riverbank of the Potomac at night,

And sang across (t t t t t t t t) to the slaves (i i i i i i) in Virginia

I cut my tongue on the cut

garnet

of tableaux dust

River folk not just because we waded in the water

Not just because when Tubman sang

“Moses go down Egypt, /

Til ole Pharao’ let me go;

Hadn’t been for Adam’s fall, /

Shouldn’t have to die at all

that meant whites were nearby

and we needed to stay hidden behind ( th th th th th th)

the trees

Not just because Moses’ name means water

“to pull out of the water”

impediment is a flowing water.”

Geschreven en gesproken taal zijn niet Ellis’ enige instrumenten. Er is ook ander, door het lichaam voortgebracht spreken. Ellis is saxofonist, pianist, zanger en vermengt muzikale improvisatie met het geschreven woord. “What if the stutter is not something I need to get rid of? Maybe I can approach it as an instrument, that I can learn to play,’’ zegt Ellis in een interview.

Maybe. Het benutten van een vermeend gebrek als creatief middel lijkt een gevestigde gedachte. Het is de aarzeling, de maybe , die doet vermoeden dat de stotter voor Ellis iets is waar steeds over onderhandeld moet worden. De hapering als praktijk waarbinnen Ellis telkens opnieuw onderzoekt wat de implicaties zijn van zo’n onderbreking. Het is niet de vraag of de stotter ‘overwonnen’ of getransformeerd kan worden tot een instrument, maar wat zich voordoet wanneer die twijfel telkens opnieuw wordt omgekeerd.

“in time rather than on time

is that

we allow ourselves

to um

to be

vessels and and

and be present

with

um

with a belief

that whatever comes

is

um

is what’s supposed to come

because it

doesn’t you know

it’s it’s not

it’s not ours.’’

Op een opname van een performance, waarbij de partituur op een groot scherm te zien is, wandelt Ellis al saxofoon spelend door het publiek. Snel merk ik dat mijn aandacht een andere afslag neemt. De aanwezigheid van Ellis brengt een ambivalente fysicaliteit teweeg. Ellis bespeelt de ruimte, maar onttrekt zich er ook aan. Alsof niet de partituur leidend is, maar de muziek het visuele in gang zet. Mens en muziek, muziek en geschreven tekst raken versmolten. Ellis wordt als het ware omhelsd door de partituur en speelt tegelijkertijd de hoofdrol. Niets ligt volledig vast: niet wat de muziek stuurt, niet waar de partituur eindigt, niet waar het lichaam van Ellis begint of ophoudt. De kruisbestuiving tussen ruimte, lichaam en muziek laat zien dat betekenis juist ontstaat waar de grenzen tussen deze werelden in elkaar overlopen.

Evenals Ellis schreef Spaink met het lichaam mee. Het lichaam niet alleen als drager van het werk, maar als een actieve voorwaarde ervan. Tot haar laatste levensdagen behield Spaink grip op de wijze waarop zij betekenis gaf aan de grootste onvermijdelijkheid van het leven. Taal als in-en uitgang.

Zolang C. nog niet is teruggekeerd blader ik verder. “Sick, blue sea” (2018) van kunstenares Lizzy Rose voert een fictieve potvis ten tonele. Aha! De walvis waar C. aan refereerde.

Ook hierbij komt het internet wanneer ik thuis ben goed van pas: het werk is online beschikbaar. Op een Tumblrblog met de naam Sickbabyblue houdt de potvis een openbaar dagboek bij. Het videokunstwerk, waarin Rose laat zien wat Sickbabyblue bezighoudt, zien we de potvis’ eerste blogpost: “One time in 2012 a sperm whale with access to the internet and a keyboard starts an online blog. She isn’t quite sure what her blog will be about. She decided to start with talking about her day, interesting things that happened, random thoughts and observations. She isn’t really expecting anyone to read it. She might share it with some of her friends. Anyway it is nice to have somewhere to unload her thoughts. It would be cool if other whales would read it she supposes; maybe they have had similar experiences? It can be a bit lonely down there in the deep blue sea.”

De film van Rose doet op het eerste oog komisch aan. Met vervormde stem horen we de potvis vertellen over haar dagen: “I didn’t have much to do today so I decided to spend the day making myself a nice dinner. I went diving again. It took me ages to find some squid, but when I finally found some I tried to suck it in.” Slurpende geluiden. “Ahhhhh, I didn’t manage to catch it. So annoying! I’m so annoyed. Why me?”

Lange tijd houdt Sickbabyblue haar humoristische toon vast. Maar ook potvissen kunnen zich niet altijd groothouden.

“I feel too sick to dive, too sick to do anything. I can’t think, I feel too sick. I cant think, I feel too sick. I hope it ends soon. When will it end?”

De film van Rose duurt slechts tien minuten, en toch weet ze de kijker volledig mee te voeren in een wereld waarin zwemmen, duiken, eten en misselijkheid elkaar afwisselen. Maar er is ook iets groters aan de hand. De zee is ook ziek. Het water raakt vervuild. Het kan zomaar gebeuren dat ze een plastic boodschappentas naar binnen slokt.

“What if whatever’s in there can’t come out? My body is trying to break it down. 450 years it takes. How long do sperm whales live? 60 years. I don’t think I can feel this sick for 60 years. Never mind 450.”

Rose doet iets wat mij vaker opvalt in het werk van kunstenaars wier fysieke bewegingsruimte beperkt is. De verbeeldingskracht, waarmee iedere kunstenaar de grenzen van het voor de hand liggende overstijgt, wordt niet alleen als artistiek middel aangesproken, maar ook tot artistiek vraagstuk verheven. Multidisciplinair kunstenaar Melvin Moti, over wie ik eerder schreef , vormt in zijn animatiefilm On A Clear Day de veranderende omstandigheden van zijn zieke geliefde om tot een fantasiewereld waarin dansende kikkers een nieuwe werkelijkheid vormen. De kikkers symboliseren in zijn film niet enkel een onberekenbare gezondheid, maar verbeelden een droom. Een droom waarin ziekte weliswaar een allesomvattende rol speelt, maar ook aangevuld wordt door al het andere van betekenis.

Moti doet, evenals Rose, een poging om ingrijpende en levensveranderende gebeurtenissen te vertalen naar een eigen taal. Het aanspreken van de verbeeldingskracht in een poging grip te krijgen op een bij vlagen onverteerbare, maar soms ook wrange of zelfs komische werkelijkheid. Een meedogenloze werkwijze: er zit niets anders op dan de realiteit recht in de ogen te kijken, te onderzoeken wat er allemaal nog meer over te zeggen valt.

Spaink, Ellis, Rose en Moti delen deze nietsontziende aanpak. Allen laten zij op eigen wijze zien dat het lichaam meer is dan een fysieke entiteit. Wanneer onbekommerd functioneren geen automatische vanzelfsprekendheid is, openen zich luikjes die door ervaring en gebrek – een oxymoron, zou je denken – ingegeven zijn.

De golfbewegingen waarmee de potvis getuigenissen de ether in slingert, blijven onbeantwoord. Geen enkele respons. Haar gedachten worden uitgesproken, maar nooit beantwoord. De ingebouwde stiltes in de film, waarin zelfs de ruis van de microfoon ontbreekt, versterken deze droevige realiteit. Sickbabyblue zoekt naar verlossing, maar juist daarin huist een paradox. Ontsnapping lijkt enkel mogelijk door eerdere uitspraken te herhalen. Steeds opnieuw. Een poging betekenis te geven aan een werkelijkheid die zich aan ieder wederwoord onttrekt.

“Nausea is quite bad today. Still feeling sick. I actually can’t think to type anything else. No thoughts. Can’t think, too sick. Can’t think, too sick. No thoughts, can’t think too sick.”

C. verschijnt weer en op datzelfde moment maakt de geroemde terrasbuurvrouw aanstalten te vertrekken. Zonder dat ik er erg in had heb ik haar ingebouwd tussen muur, deur en mijzelf.

Wanneer ik vraag of ik iets kan doen om haar vertrek te vlotten – eerder leidde opzij gaan tot beleefd protest en onmiddellijk dwarsbomen van protest is nooit een goed idee – kijkt ze me ondeugend aan: “Eerst opstaan. Op mijn leeftijd is dat nog een kunst.”
excerpt_original: Lichamelijke tekortkomingen omkeren en naar hun hand te zetten, getuigen van hun onmogelijke werkelijkheid. Dat doen de kunstenaars die Mira Thompson voor Mister Motley voor het voetlicht bracht binnen haar reeks Land zonder grenzen. Vandaag sluit ze de serie af met een essay…

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jonk 是世界上最受赞誉的废墟摄影师之一。十多年来，他一直在全球各地寻找这些地方。在他的第十二本书《Urbex Stories》中，他带我们踏上了穿越七个国家的二十个真实故事的冒险之旅。一条狗、一把步枪、一把刀、一记重拳、一个警报器、一名警卫、警察、一次跌倒、捉迷藏：这些只是这本书的其中一些元素，它们能让你跟随他一同完全沉浸在引人入胜的废墟探险（urbex）世界中。Jonk 写道：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自2025年春天以来，一些幸运儿已经能够加入我在废墟探险之旅（Urbex Tours）中的废墟探索。在为期四到六天的时间里，在四人组成的小型团组中，我提供了一场深入体验我作为废墟猎人工作的沉浸式旅程。这本书是一种将更多人带入废墟探险这个非常特殊的世界的方式，这个世界如此引人入胜，对某些人来说又如此令人恐惧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过《Urbex Stories》，我想揭示我的照片背后的故事。无论是通过寻找地点、旅行、实地考察，还是后期制作以及摄影师的生活，我都试图挑选出能够为读者提供我的世界全景的故事。当然，大多数故事都集中在参观本身以及它们带来的冒险经历上。从遇到业主或保安，到遭遇看门狗或野生动物，再到与武器的接触或险些发生物理事故，在社交媒体、书籍或展览中看到的影像背后，其实发生了许多事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所有这一切只是这里讲述的二十个故事的一部分；其余的我会留作惊喜。不过还是有一个剧透警告：你会发现一个对《美国X档案》（American History X）的致敬，至今仍让我不寒而栗；还有在意大利遇到的一些绝对算不上友善的俄罗斯人、一记重拳、一个妓女、一个警报器、损坏的设备、种族主义……简而言之，这些内容足以让你想要加入我的旅行团！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过这本书，我也希望能分享我对古老石头的喜爱，以及我对时间流逝并在万物上留下痕迹这一奇观的热情。这种磨损和腐朽的铜绿、我不断提及但在此将再次书写的逝去时间的标记：生锈的铁块、剥落的油漆、灰尘、碎玻璃，当然还有大自然收复失地，共同构成了绝妙的场景。至少对我而言是这样，我希望当你合上这本书时，你也是如此。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "祝阅读愉快，并享受沉浸在我的世界中的乐趣！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jonk", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这本书可以从法国的任何书店、任何在线书店订购，也可以在 Jonk 或 Editions Tempus Fugit 的网站上订购签名版或亲笔签名副本。它包含在8个国家拍摄的122张照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jonk : Urbex Stories 出版社：Editions Tempus Fugit 出版时间：2026年10月 平装本 – 164页 语言：法语 规格：16 cm x 22 cm ISBN：978-2-9590720-2-4 价格：€29", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://editionstempusfugit.fr/", "links": [{"text": "https://editionstempusfugit.fr/", "url": "https://editionstempusfugit.fr/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "http://www.jonk-photography.com", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Jonk is one of the world’s most acclaimed photographers of abandoned places. For more than ten years, he has been traveling the globe in search of them. In this twelfth book, Urbex Storie s, he takes us along on his adventures through twenty true stories set in seven countries. A dog, a rifle, a knife, a punch, an alarm, a guard, the police, a fall, hide-and-seek: these are just some of the ingredients that make this book a total immersion at his side in the fascinating world of urbex. Jonk writes:

Since the spring of 2025, a lucky few have been able to join me in the wastelands on my Urbex Tours. Over periods of four to six days, in small groups of four, I offer an immersion into my work as a ruin hunter. This book is a way of taking more people with me into the very particular world of urbex, so intriguing, and so frightening for some.

With Urbex Stories , I want to reveal what lies behind my photos. Whether through searching for locations, travelling, on-site approaches, but also post-processing and the life of a photographer, I have tried to select stories that give the reader a complete panorama of my world. Of course, most of the stories focus on the visits themselves and the adventures they brought. From meeting an owner or a security guard to encountering a guard dog or wild animals, by way of experiences with weapons or narrowly avoided physical accidents, a lot happens behind an image seen on social media, in books or in exhibitions.

All of this is only part of the twenty stories told here; I’ll leave the rest be a surprise. Spoiler alert nonetheless: you’ll find a reference to American History X that still sends a chill down my spine, some decidedly unfriendly Russians met in Italy, a punch, a prostitute, an alarm, broken equipment, racism… in short, enough to make you want to join me on my Tours!

Through this book, I also hope to share my taste for old stones, and my passion for the spectacle of time passing and leaving its mark on everything. This patina of wear and decay, these markers of time gone by that I never stop citing but will write down once more here: rusted iron, peeling paint, dust, broken glass and, of course, nature taking back its place, create fabulous settings. For me, at least, and I hope for you too when you close this book.

Happy reading, and enjoy the immersion into my world!

Jonk

The book can be ordered from any bookstore in France, from any online bookstore, or on the websites of Jonk or Editions Tempus Fugit for a signed or autographed copy. It contains 122 photographs taken in 8 countries.

title_original: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours

The athletes may be long gone but the legacy of the sporting spectacle rolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.", "links": [{"text": "legacy of the sporting spectacle", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2022/jun/30/a-massive-betrayal-how-londons-olympic-legacy-was-sold-out"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of the Yard theatre . Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.", "links": [{"text": "Yard theatre", "url": "https://www.theyardtheatre.co.uk/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – and Ian McKellen set to star in the next show .", "links": [{"text": "Ian McKellen set to star in the next show", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/may/14/ian-mckellen-king-lear-yard-theatre-east-london"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/38335427cc214ab877b18493562429cdd84b7a3e/178_0_5355_4284/master/5355.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Empty curved auditorium at the Yard theatre, with tiered grey seating facing a brick-walled stage", "caption": "Will the actors’ knees be able to take it? … the concrete stage. Photograph: Oliver Wainwright", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates of Practice Architecture to conjure an ad hoc auditorium on a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.", "links": [{"text": "Practice Architecture", "url": "https://practicearchitecture.co.uk/project/the-yard-theatre/"}, {"text": "ad hoc auditorium", "url": "https://practicearchitecture.co.uk/project/the-yard-theatre/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard into a mixed-use district . That project never materialised, but Miller succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (Community Infrastructure Levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.", "links": [{"text": "a mixed-use district", "url": "https://www.stockwool.co.uk/our-projects/residential/queens-yard/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0af8f9a59adeaa837989bced823baabf6f0a2f2f/0_472_5179_4143/master/5179.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "The Yard Theatre’s brick facade with faded lettering above a glass entrance door", "caption": "Spell it out … the theatre’s name in the multicoloured recycled brickwork. Photograph: Oliver Wainwright", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work of Takero Shimazaki , a Tokyo-born Londoner who was shortlisted for the Stirling prize last year for an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. article_text:
S ince the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but the legacy of the sporting spectacle rolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.

But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of the Yard theatre . Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.

It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – and Ian McKellen set to star in the next show .

“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates of Practice Architecture to conjure an ad hoc auditorium on a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.

Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard into a mixed-use district . That project never materialised, but Miller succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (Community Infrastructure Levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.

The resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work of Takero Shimazaki , a Tokyo-born Londoner who was shortlisted for the Stirling prize last year for an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. It reads like a collage of its context: a shed clad with corrugated fibre-cement sheeting, rising from graffiti-covered warehouse walls on one side and framed by a new brick gable end on the other. The bricks include subtle shades of blue, yellow and magenta, in a nod to the previous printworks, while the name of the theatre is spelt out in the brickwork, recalling the faded factory signs of the area. In keeping with the waste-not ethos, these K-Briqs , manufactured in Scotland, are unfired and made of 95% construction waste, recycling 16 tonnes of waste that would have otherwise gone to landfill and saving the equivalent of 3.5 tonnes of CO 2 that regular bricks would have emitted.

There is a grandeur to the new theatre’s form. With its central tower and symmetrical pitch roof, Shimazaki says the Yard was inspired by Palladian churches to bring a sense of permanence, as if the building might have been here far longer than it has. “The Yard was interested in the idea of permanence in theatre, and fakery in architecture,” he says. “And how to build something grownup with not much money.” Mirrored panels in some of the windows bring a theatrical touch, while bright pink guttering and yellow coping blend with the local street art vernacular. Miraculously, for now, the new brickwork remains graffiti free.

Entering through big double doors – emblazoned with “open me up now” – you find a large open foyer and cafe, with walls and banquettes in rich shades of burgundy, while a glossy blue bar is framed with bands of teal and green, recalling a Josef Albers painting. Gold-painted columns add a touch of theatrical bling, which will be cranked up a notch next year when a vestibule is installed. Designed by artist Ed Atkins , it will usher theatregoers through a dramatic ruched silver curtain. The loos add further sparkle, inspired by the bathroom at the Villa Necchi Campiglio in Milan , with glossy black tiles, shiny brass fittings and coloured lino floors – “a little bit of economical opulence”, as Shimazaki puts it.

So what of the theatre itself? A central staircase leads up through a dark passage to the new auditorium, where the architects had to strike a tricky balance. “We wanted to retain what people loved about the old space,” says Miller, “and evolve what wasn’t as functional.” It has the same bare bones quality as before, with an exposed back wall built with bricks salvaged from the site, a concrete stage (actors’ knees won’t thank them), and curved, raked seating in the manner of an amphitheatre. The plastic cafe seats were upgraded for upholstered communal benches.

“Epic and intimate at the same time” was the brief, and Shimazaki has risen to the challenge, creating a 250-capacity space – more than double the previous theatre – that is at once cosy and grand. Continuing the fakery theme, the cast concrete-looking seating structure is actually cement particle board, while banks of radiators hidden below the seats keep bums warm while aiding the passive stack ventilation system. As before, what you see is what you get: there are no wings, no fly tower, nowhere for the actors to hide. “We wanted to amplify the sense of liveness,” says Miller. “After all, that’s what makes theatre unique.” It still feels raw – although performers now benefit from the luxury of dressing rooms, tucked beneath the seating, saving them from dashing to beat the audience to the loos in the interval.

Around the other side of the building, the graffitied warehouse offices are being transformed into a youth hub by Jeremy Deller and architect educators Matt+Fiona, alongside local schoolchildren. It’s part of an Arts Council-funded series that has also seen an Antony Gormley figure appear on the roof – visible from the elevated platform of Hackney Wick station – with further commissions and community collaborations in the works.

The ad hoc ingenuity on show puts what is emerging across the other side of the park into sharp relief. One of the biggest components of the Olympic legacy is the “cultural quarter” of East Bank in Stratford, a £1.1bn colossus that houses branches of the V&A, Sadler’s Wells theatre, BBC studios, University of the Arts London and University College London, soon to be garnished with towers of unaffordable flats. The presence of these institutions is welcome – but despite the big budgets, top architects and endless design review panels, the results feel less than world class.

It is a cumbersome beast, designed by committee and airlifted in from on high, begat from the loins of mayors hungry for legacies. The Yard, by contrast, shows how a young, agile team with a fraction of the resources can achieve so much, building a project that feels truly grown from its place.

editorial_title_zh: 内森·菲尔德本来不应该出现在《You Can See Everything》中
editorial_excerpt_zh: 兰斯·奥彭海姆向 IndieWire 讲述了这部纪录片在制作头几天如何发生了根本性的方向转变，包括菲尔德决定联合执导、出镜，并彻底改变了拍摄方式。

Heaven", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/some-kind-of-heaven-review-darren-aronofsky-the-villages-1234609430/"}, {"text": "Ren Faire,", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/ren-faire-how-lance-oppenheim-filmed-hbo-series-1235118740/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“[在我之前的两部纪录片中]我有兴趣沉浸在某种主体性中，并使用大量的电影工具和行话技巧，让观众关心我片中合作对象的愿望、需求以及他们所面临的障碍，”奥彭海姆说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其结果是，这些非虚构项目在外观和感觉上往往像有剧本的叙事电影，具有表现力地运用了电影形式。（你可以在此处阅读更多关于奥彭海姆在《文艺复兴展》中的纪录片幻想曲方法的信息。）", "links": [{"text": "here", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/hbo-ren-faire-behind-the-scenes-1235012137/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当我们第一次到达[霍姆斯和埃文斯位于德尔玛的海滩小屋]时，我非常坚定，‘内森，你知道的，我的工作方式非常独特，’”奥彭海姆说。“我用一台摄像机工作。我喜欢用变形镜头拍摄——它对图像和过程产生了我喜欢的效果——而他说，‘好吧，行，我们试试那个。’", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个需要一个小团队的过程，最多四到六人，倾向于对场景进行具体而坚决的构图，而不是像大多数纪录片那样用多台摄像机捕捉展开的动作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/YCSE_BTS-2.png?w=650", "alt": "《You Can See Everything》片场中的兰斯·奥彭海姆和内森·菲尔德", "caption": "克里斯·马焦拍摄的《You Can See Everything》片场照中的兰斯·奥彭海姆和内森·菲尔德", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“内森已经很久没有以这种身份工作了，可能自从他在加拿大的短片以来就没有过了，”奥彭海姆说。他还指出了这位《寻堡奇遇》和《顶包 rehearsal》创作者可以说最大的变化：“他原本也不打算为此出镜。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在海滩隐蔽处拍摄霍姆斯和埃文斯时，奥彭海姆既定方法的缺陷从一开始就显露无遗。“变形[镜头]只持续了一天左右，”奥彭海姆说。“我们最初开始时采用了更宽的宽高比。那行不通。我们意识到他们的生活极其局限于这间房子里，因为害怕狗仔队拍到他们的照片。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同样成问题的是只使用一台摄像机，奥彭海姆称其为“一场灾难”——这场灾难当时正端坐在摄像机后面的菲尔德立即注意到了。“每次伊丽莎白和比利移动时，我们的[摄像机]操作员都会手忙脚乱地去追赶他们，”奥彭海姆解释道。“我们不是手持拍摄，它总是在支架[三脚架]上，所以我们不得不更换镜头，或者不得不加上一个附加镜，然后我们就会完全错过这个时刻。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是在这种需要进行摄像机调整的停停走走的过程中，有趣的事情开始发生了。“当摄像机操作员在更换东西时，伊丽莎白和比利会问内森问题，”奥彭海姆说。“然后摄像机重新开机，[并且]他们会继续问内森问题。感觉他们几乎把内森拉到了摄像机前面，这真的很有趣。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据奥彭海姆称，到拍摄第二天，菲尔德开始出现在镜头前，但只是“断断续续的”，但随着菲尔德被拉入画面的频率越来越高，“[内森对我说]，‘其实，你知道吗？我们应该一起导演这个，’”他说。“而我说，‘你他妈在开玩笑吧？当然。我也想要这样。’”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MCDYOCA_EC125.jpg?w=650", "alt": "《You Can See Everything》中的内森·菲尔德。", "caption": "《You Can See Everything》中的内森·菲尔德 A24/由 Everett Collection 提供", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如 IndieWire 此前报道的那样，奥彭海姆、菲尔德及其团队在早期对他们所看到的东西感到迷惑不解——这对夫妇近距离的行为只引发了更多的问题，引发了电影制作团队对如何解读他们所看到的东西的分歧（看过《You Can See Everything》的观众很可能会对此产生共鸣）。电影制作人发现，当菲尔德在镜头前时，他们可以更充分地探究和探索这种困惑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“是他们把[内森]拉了进去，向他提问，征求他对事情的看法，然后在他意识到这一点后，也许觉得这是一个机会，至少可以把那些让他感到困惑、也让我们感到困惑的所见所闻提出来，”奥彭海姆说道。“然后，一旦[菲尔德开始更频繁地出现在镜头前]，我们就觉得：‘好吧，我们得想出一套新的拍法。这种单机位的方法行不通。’\"", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "宽银幕变形镜头不见了，奥彭海姆转而使用更常规的纪录片变焦镜头和更紧凑的 4:3 画幅，“[这让我们]能够真正沉浸在这些面部的瞬间里，这似乎是我们现在最感兴趣的，仅仅是去观察细微差别、微表情，”奥彭海姆说道。“这也让环境得以改变，所以如果我们被困在这所房子里，[更紧凑的画幅会让]这个空间感觉稍微大了一点。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "菲尔德坚持认为他们在这间海滩小屋里需要多台摄像机——这里发生的事情太多了，捕捉埃文斯、霍姆斯和他自己（以及后来的霍姆斯的父母）之间的小瞬间和微表情，对这个项目至关重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "解决方案是两名摄像师，各使用一支变焦镜头，每天在房子的不同区域拍摄 14 到 16 小时。由于摄像机经常对准霍姆斯和埃文斯的脸，奥彭海姆担心他们会错过更大空间的动态，以及某人离开房间的时刻。解决办法是使用第三台配备 12mm（超广角）镜头的摄像机，由奥彭海姆本人操作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据奥彭海姆所说，这种拍摄纪录片方法的重大转变，加上菲尔德与霍姆斯和埃文斯的互动，使得《You Can See Everything》的制作团队找到了节奏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MCDYOCA_EC124.jpg?w=650", "alt": "《YOU CANSEE EVERYTHING》，从左至右：导演内森·菲尔德，伊丽莎白·霍姆斯，2026年。© A24 / 由 Everett Collection 提供", "caption": "《You Can See Everything》 由 Everett Collection 提供", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“一旦我们能够进行超长时间的拍摄，伊丽莎白和比利就好像真的不再——对某个瞬间没有任何压力了；感觉不像是我们在做一个[类似于]传统的采访。我们基本上能够让他们的生活自然上演，并在几乎完全不知道我们对什么感兴趣的情况下追踪一切，”奥彭海姆说道。“而对瞬间没有压力，使得内森能够在[霍姆斯和埃文斯]尽可能不戒备的情况下提出问题，这才是真正的突破。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奥彭海姆表示，他和菲尔德早在考虑制作一部关于伊丽莎白·霍姆斯的电影之前就已建立的创作默契，源于一种对“捕捉真实生活的挑战”的兴趣。回想起来，他认为他们应对霍姆斯这一挑战的解决方案需要两位导演都跳出各自的固有方法，因为所需要做的是“把观众带进那个房间里，带入身临其境的体验中”。与其说创造一种增强角色主观性的镜头，或是一种带有诠释或幽默色彩的镜头，不如说它是为了邀请观众去体验他们在观察这对伴侣时所感到的“认知失调”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“对我来说，这是一种非常不同的工作方式，我想对内森也是如此。我们不得不去学习彼此的语言，通过这样做，我认为我们在艺术上开辟了新天地，”奥彭海姆说道。“本质上，我们最终创作的是[内森]或我所能制作的最严谨的真实纪录片（vérité documentary）形式，而这所需要的，实际上就是身处现场、进行观察，并试着对随时突然呈现在眼前的那些事情作出有机反应。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "想要收听兰斯·奥彭海姆的完整采访，请在 Apple、Spotify 或你喜爱的播客平台上订阅 Filmmaker Toolkit 播客。你还可以在 YouTube 上观看完整采访。", "links": [{"text": "Filmmaker Toolkit podcast", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/filmmaker-toolkit-podcast/"}, {"text": "Apple", "url": "https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/indiewires-filmmaker-toolkit/id1142632832"}, {"text": "Spotify", "url": "https://open.spotify.com/show/2cfkvzAeM8BFxkCo58Qs8G"}, {"text": "YouTube", "url": Co-directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder came aboard the documentary project just weeks before its subject, Elizabeth Holmes, was scheduled to report to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryant, Texas, to serve an 11-year sentence for defrauding her Theranos investors.", "links": [{"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/you-can-see-everything/"}, {"text": "Lance Oppenheim", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/primetime-cinematography-explained-colonoscopy-camera-robert-pattinson-1235219102/"}, {"text": "Nathan Fielder", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/podcast/you-can-see-everything-how-documentary-came-together-1235222750/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While, as IndieWire previously reported , Fielder was deeply skeptical there was a film to be made with Holmes and her partner Billy Evans. (He even negotiated a “ kill switch ” in his deal with A24, permitting him to abandon the project at any point.) article_text:
“ You Can See Everything ” came together very quickly. Co-directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder came aboard the documentary project just weeks before its subject, Elizabeth Holmes, was scheduled to report to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryant, Texas, to serve an 11-year sentence for defrauding her Theranos investors.

While, as IndieWire previously reported , Fielder was deeply skeptical there was a film to be made with Holmes and her partner Billy Evans. (He even negotiated a “ kill switch ” in his deal with A24, permitting him to abandon the project at any point.) From the start, however, he did see it as an opportunity to collaborate with Oppenheim — not unlike what he did with Benny Safdie on “The Curse” — a director with his own distinct approach to capturing reality.

“Nathan was very adamant from the jump with me, ‘I’m going to produce this, you’re going to direct this,’” said Oppenheim on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast . “And then he’s like, ‘I want to be there, though, and I want to see how you do it. I want to see how you work.’”

Oppenheim’s previous three nonfiction projects, “ Some Kind of Heaven ,” “Spermworld,” and the HBO series “ Ren Faire, ” were what the director describes as “docu-fantasies.”

“[In my previous three documentaries] I was interested in inhabiting a subjectivity and using a lot of cinematic tools and tricks of the trade to get an audience to care about the wants and needs and the obstacles for the participants I was working with in the film,” said Oppenheim.

The result is non-fiction projects that often look and feel like scripted narrative films, using the cinematic form expressively. (You can read more here about Oppenheim’s docu-fantasy approach on “Ren Faire.”)

“When we first got [to Holmes and Evans’ Del Mar beach cottage], I was very adamant, ‘Nathan, you know, I work in a very specific sort of way,’” said Oppenheim. “I work with one camera. I like to shoot anamorphically — it does something to the image and process that I like — and he was like, ‘OK, yeah, let’s try that.’

It’s a process that involves a small crew, four to six people maximum, with a preference for a specific and determined composition of a scene, rather than, like on most documentaries, covering the unfolding action with multiple cameras.

“Nathan hadn’t worked in this capacity in a really long time, maybe not since his short films in Canada,” said Oppenheim. He also noted arguably the biggest change for the “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal” creator: “He wasn’t planning to be on camera for this too.”

When it came to capturing Holmes and Evans in their beachside hideaway, the flaws of Oppenheim’s established approach became apparent right from the jump. “The anamorphic [lensing] lasted for about a day,” said Oppenheim. “We initially started with a wider aspect ratio. That wasn’t working. We realized that their life was extremely confined to this house because out of fear of paparazzi taking their pictures.”

Equally problematic was using only one camera, which Oppheim said “was a disaster” — a disaster Fielder, now perched behind the camera, picked up on immediately. “Every time Elizabeth and Billy would move our [camera] operators would struggle to catch up with them,” explained Oppenheim. “We weren’t shooting handheld, it was always on sticks [a tripod], so we’d have to switch lenses, or we’d have to throw a diopter on, and then we would miss the moment completely.”

It was during this stop and start process of needing to make camera adjustments, something interesting started to happen. “While the camera operators were changing things, Elizabeth and Billy would ask Nathan questions,” said Oppenheim. “And then the camera would come back on, [and] they’d continue asking Nathan questions. It felt like they were drawing Nathan almost in front of the camera, which was really interesting.”

According to Oppenheim, by the second day of filming, Fielder would start to appear on camera, but only in “fits and starts,” but as Fielder got pulled on screen with increasing frequency, “[Nathan said to me], ‘Actually, you know what? We should direct this together,'” he said. “And I was like, ‘Are you fucking kidding me? Of course. I want that, too.’”

As IndieWire has previously reported, Oppenheim, Fielder, and crew were befuddled early on by what they were observing — the couple’s behavior up-close only raised more questions, sparking disagreements among the filmmaking team of how to interpret what they were seeing (an experience audiences who have seen “You Can See Everything” are likely able to relate to). The filmmakers discovered they could probe and explore that confusion more fully with Fielder on camera.

“It was them pulling [Nathan] in, asking him questions, asking him his opinion on things, and then him also realizing, once that started happening, maybe there was an opportunity to at least bring up the things he was observing that were confusing to him, that were also confusing to us,” said Oppenheim. “Then once [Fielder started to appear more frequently on camera], we were like, ‘OK, we have to come up with a new system of doing stuff. This one camera approach doesn’t work.’”

Gone were the widescreen anamorphic lenses, as Oppenheim shifted to more standard documentary zoom lenses and a tighter 4:3 aspect ratio, which “[allowed us] to actually live in these moments on faces, which is seemingly what is most interesting to us right now, just seeing the nuances, the microexpressions,” said Oppenheim. “It also helps the environment change, so if we’re stuck in this house, [the tighter aspect ratio makes] it feel like maybe the space is a little bigger.”

Fielder insisted they needed multiple cameras in the beach cottage — there was too much going on, and capturing the small moments and micro-expressions between Evans, Holmes, and himself (and eventually Holmes’ parents) became vital to the project.

The solution was two camera operators, each on a zoom lens, shooting from different parts of the house for 14 to 16 hours a day. Because the cameras were often zoomed in on Holmes and Evans’ faces, Oppenheim worried they would miss the dynamics of the larger space, as well as moments when someone left the room. The solution was a third camera with a 12mm (extremely wide) lens, operated by Oppenheim himself.

According to Oppenheim, this significant shift in the approach to shooting the documentary, in conjunction with Fielder’s interaction with Holmes and Evans, allowed the “You Can See Everything” filmmaking team to find its rhythm.

“Once we were able to shoot for really long periods of time, it felt like both Elizabeth and Billy didn’t really — there was no pressure on a moment; it didn’t feel like we were doing something [akin] to a traditional interview. We were able to basically let their lives play out and follow almost everything without really knowing what we were interested in,” said Oppenheim. “And the lack of pressure on the moment made it so that Nathan was able to actually ask questions without [Holmes and Evans], as much as possible, [having] their guards up, and that was the real breakthrough.”

Oppenheim said his creative bond with Fielder, dating back to well before they considered making an Elizabeth Holmes film, was an interest “in the challenges of capturing authentic life.” Looking back, he thinks their solution to this challenge with Holmes required both filmmakers to step out of their respective approaches, because what was needed was “to bring the audience into that room, into the experience of being there.” Rather than creating a lens that heightened the subjectivity of the characters, or one of interpretation or humor, it was about inviting the audience to experience the “cognitive dissonance” they were having while observing the couple.

“For me it was a very different way of working, and for Nathan as well, I think. We had to sort of learn the language of each other, and in doing that, we were able to, I think, break new ground artistically,” said Oppenheim. “Essentially what we ended up creating is the most rigorous form of a vérité documentary that [Nathan] or I could have ever made, and what that entailed was really just being present, observing, trying to organically respond to things that jumped out at us at any given moment.”

excerpt_original: Lance Oppenheim tells IndieWire how the documentary radically changed course in the first few days of production, including Fielder deciding to co-direct, appear on camera, and completely alter how it was shot.
